title: Daily Notebooks
text:
Editing these notebooks
The .ipynb files are edited directly — open one, change a cell, run it, save. Two kinds of cell are the exception: the 📦 Setup cell and each 🔧 Library cell are built from _notebook_lib.py, so that a helper used on several days has one definition and a day imports only what it uses. Those cells say so in their own second line, and editing them by hand does not last. To change a helper’s code, edit _notebook_lib.py; to change which helpers a cell ships, edit that cell’s lda2 metadata. Then run the sync below.
The helpers sit at the end of _notebook_lib.py as ordinary Python, one # === name :: caption === section each. Edit one the way you would edit any function — nothing there is quoted text, and nothing runs it locally.
Two scripts sit next to the notebooks:
python sources/notebooks/_sync_notebooks.py    # rebuild those cells, clear outputs
python sources/notebooks/_check_notebooks.py   # every cell compiles, fits a screen, is introduced
Run both before committing. _sync_notebooks.py --check reports what would change without writing anything, and --notebook day3 limits it to one file.
Notebooks are committed without outputs, so their diffs stay readable. A git filter takes the outputs out on the way into a commit and leaves your working copy untouched. Filters are per-clone configuration, so turn it on once in a fresh clone:
git config filter.nbstrip.clean "uv run python sources/notebooks/_sync_notebooks.py --stdin-strip"
To search the prose across all five notebooks, read the cell sources rather than the JSON:
jq -r '.cells[].source | add' sources/notebooks/*.ipynb | grep -i "confusion matrix"

title: Day 4 · Pipeline assembly & sampling your gold set
section: Part A · Tutorial — sample a balanced gold subset
text:
Part A · Tutorial — sample a balanced gold subset
For your mini-project you build your own gold set by sampling from a pool. A balanced sample (equal items per label) keeps precision/recall/F1 and the confusion matrix meaningful. Here we demo it on the familiar CEFR pool; swap POOL_URL for your track’s pool. See the mini-project tracks for the full list.

Setup — run this first


Show code
#@title 📦 Setup — run me first { display-mode: "form" }
# Helper — you don't need to read this. Run it and move on.
# Generated from _notebook_lib.py — edit there, not here; changes to this cell are replaced.
import json, urllib.request

print("Setup done.")




Show code
#@title 🔧 Library cell: load_gold { display-mode: "form" }
# Helper — you don't need to read this. Run it and move on.
# Generated from _notebook_lib.py — edit there, not here; changes to this cell are replaced.
#   load_gold(url_or_path) → gold

def load_gold(url_or_path: str) -> list[dict[str, str]]:
    """Read the canonical gold JSON: [{'id','text','label'}, ...].

    Args:
        url_or_path: a web address, or the path to a file on this machine.

    Returns:
        The gold items, each a dict with "id", "text" and "label".

    Example:
        >>> gold = load_gold(GOLD_URL)
    """
    if str(url_or_path).startswith("http"):                 # a web address?
        raw = urllib.request.urlopen(url_or_path).read().decode("utf-8")  # download it
        gold = json.loads(raw)                              # JSON text -> list of dicts
    else:                                                   # otherwise a file on disk
        gold = json.loads(open(url_or_path, encoding="utf-8").read())
    print(f"Loaded {len(gold)} items. First one:", gold[0])  # proof it worked
    return gold




Show code
POOL_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/egumasa/linguistic-data-analysis-II-2026/main/sources/resources/datasets/gold/cefr_pool_demo.json"   # ✏️ swap for your track's pool
pool = load_gold(POOL_URL)   # the big labelled set you will sample FROM




Draw a balanced sample ✏️ YOU EDIT
PER_LABEL items per label, with a fixed random seed so the sample is reproducible (same every run). Rare classes simply yield fewer — that’s a property of the data.


Show code
import random
from collections import defaultdict, Counter

### Step 1: the two settings you control ###
PER_LABEL = 8            # how many items per label
random.seed(42)         # fixed seed = same sample every run

### Step 2: sort the whole pool into one bucket per label ###
by_label = defaultdict(list)   # a dict that starts each new key at []
for item in pool:
    by_label[item["label"]].append(item)   # drop the item in its label's bucket

### Step 3: shuffle each bucket and take the first PER_LABEL from it ###
gold = []
for label in sorted(by_label):        # sorted() = same label order every run
    bucket = by_label[label]
    random.shuffle(bucket)            # mix, so we are not taking the first 8 found
    gold.extend(bucket[:PER_LABEL])   # a rare label simply gives fewer than 8

### Step 4: mix the labels together and renumber the ids from 1 ###
random.shuffle(gold)             # so the labels are not grouped in blocks
gold = [{"id": i + 1, "text": x["text"], "label": x["label"]}
        for i, x in enumerate(gold)]   # enumerate gives (position, item) pairs

### Step 5: report what you actually got, label by label ###
print("sampled:", len(gold), "| per label:",
      dict(Counter(x["label"] for x in gold)))   # Counter tallies the labels




Save your gold set to Google Drive
Keep your own gold set in your Drive (not the course repo). See Housing your data in Google Drive for the mount → save → load round-trip.


Show code

# import json
# with open("/content/drive/MyDrive/my_gold.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:

title: Day 4 · Pipeline assembly & sampling your gold set
section: Part B · Draw the line: which items you may look at
text:
Part B · Draw the line: which items you may look at
On Day 3 you worked with two files: val, which every prompt was scored against, and gold, opened once at the end. They were handed to you already separated. Your own gold set arrives in one piece, so drawing that line is now a step you take — and it is the last one before the model gets involved.








what it is for




dev
the items you may look at. Change the prompt because of what you see here, as often as you like.


test
opened once, at the end. Whatever it says is what you report.



The reason is the one Day 3 gave you: a score measured on the items you kept adjusting against stops measuring how good your prompt is and starts measuring how long you kept adjusting. It only ever goes up.
Both halves come out of the same annotation work, so the split costs you no extra annotation. What it costs is items you are allowed to learn from.

Split it, keeping every label on both sides ✏️ YOU EDIT
Not a straight cut down the middle: split within each label, the same bucket-then-slice shape you wrote ten minutes ago. A straight cut on a shuffled list can leave a whole label on one side, and a label missing from test drops out of your macro average without announcing itself.


Show code
### Step 1: the setting you control ###
DEV_PER_LABEL = 3       # ✏️ how many items per label you may look at

### Step 2: sort the sample into one bucket per label (as in Part A) ###
buckets = defaultdict(list)
for item in gold:
    buckets[item["label"]].append(item)

### Step 3: take the first few of each bucket for dev, the rest for test ###
dev = []
test = []
for label in sorted(buckets):
    bucket = buckets[label]
    dev.extend(bucket[:DEV_PER_LABEL])    # the ones you may look at
    test.extend(bucket[DEV_PER_LABEL:])   # everything after them

### Step 4: read the counts BEFORE you go any further ###
print("dev :", len(dev),  "|", dict(Counter(x["label"] for x in dev)))
print("test:", len(test), "|", dict(Counter(x["label"] for x in test)))


Read those two lines rather than glancing at them. A label showing up in dev with nothing left in test cannot appear in the score you report, and right now it costs you one number to fix. Later it costs an afternoon.
There is no right size for dev, only one you can defend. A bigger dev gives you steadier feedback while you iterate and leaves a smaller test, so the number you finally report bounces around more. A smaller dev means prompt decisions made on very few items — which is how you tune to noise and then watch the gain evaporate on the half you held back.
In the final project this is split_dev_test(gold, DEV, seed=SEED), and it handles the two fiddly cases this cell does not: a proportion instead of a fixed count, and a label with a single surviving item — which it sends to test, for the reason above. The rule it follows is the one you just wrote.

02b_add_samples

agreement, adjudication, and the split you wrote in Part B

the held-out run, once

03_annotate does properly what you did by hand on Day 2 (S5): two of you label the sheet independently, you measure agreement, and you adjudicate the rows you disagreed on. What comes out is your gold set, and it is what the model gets scored against — so those disagreements are doing real work, not bookkeeping.
Today is why you can read those notebooks: sample_pool is the Part-A cell in one call and split_dev_test is the Part-B cell in one call. You have seen what they do, so you can say what they do.
Before you run anything that calls the model, your group needs a signed PLAN.md — see the Final Project pages.

title: Linguistic Data Analysis II
text:
Linguistic Data Analysis II is a five-day intensive master-level graduate course on critically evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) for linguistic analysis, offered at the Graduate School of International Cultural Studies, Tohoku University, in Summer 2026.
Among broad applications of LLMs, we cover topics that allows one to empirically evaluate LLMs performance on tasks at hand. To this end, we explore annotation scheme design, gold-standard dataset construction, prompt design/tuning, and evaluation.
Given the intensive nature of the 5-day course, we focus on the core concepts, methodology, and hands-on applications, instead of helping you to fully develop your own research agenda in this domain. However, the course aims to equip the students to explore further issues in LLM through applied linguistics lens, and plan and execute research studies of their own if they are interested.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
Agenda
This is a guided, run-along session using Part A of the Day 1 notebook, in eight short steps. The model comes first and stays first: you call it, then learn just enough Python to read and score what it gives back.

Run a cell — sign in, cells and the runtime, Shift+Enter.
Read an error — run a cell that fails on purpose, and read the last line.
Variables — store a value under a name with =.
Your first LLM call — the setup cell (one import), then five prompts: the task itself, asking for a format, the same prompt twice, and one the model gets wrong.
f-strings — drop a sentence into a prompt with f"...{sentence}", then write a .format() template of your own.
What kind of value is the answer? — type(), and the three types you use all week.
Put the answer in a record — decide a sentence’s level yourself, then ask the model the same question and store both in one {id, text, label} record.
Indexing and slicing — items[2]["label"], items[:2], and comparing the two answers with ==.

Control flow (for, if, elif, functions), counting, and text segmentation come next, in Session 3.

This intensive 5-day course covers LLM-based linguistic data analysis — annotation and gold-standard construction, prompt design, and evaluation (precision/recall/F1, confusion matrices) — through lectures, tutorials, and hands-on practice, culminating in a group mini-project presentation.

What we’ll do

Introduction to LLMs & NLP Tasks
What LLMs are and how they fit linguistic analysis; the NLP tasks we’ll tackle; course overview and self-introductions.

Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
Google Colab onboarding — sign in, run a cell, read an error — then your first ai.generate_text(...) call, the data types it returns, and building a prompt with an f-string.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Place a linguistic annotation task in the classic NLP taxonomy — identify · extract · categorize, organized by unit of analysis.
Describe the NLP evaluation workflow (gold → predictions → metrics), and explain how it transfers from a trained model to a prompted LLM.
Operationalize a linguistic category into an annotation scheme with coding guidelines.
Explain inter-annotator agreement: percent agreement, why Cohen’s κ corrects for chance, and when to use quadratic weighted κ for ordered labels.
Read a confusion matrix and compute precision, recall, and F1 from its four cells (TP · TN · FP · FN).

The message of the day: labelled data is only trustworthy if the category is operationalized and two coders agree beyond chance.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Agenda
A · What NLP tasks are there — what annotation is, and the task taxonomy made concrete with linguistic examples: part of speech, word sense disambiguation, syntactic dependency, stance, and discourse moves. Tasks organized by unit and output — token-level sequence labelling, span categorization, and one label per unit. This course focuses on sentence and text categorization, where the evaluation code is manageable and the {id, text, label} shape from Session 3 is enough; span tasks bring boundary and partial-match problems that do not fit five days.
B · How NLP evaluates a system — and how it transfers to LLMs — the evaluation workflow, and what changes when you swap a trained model for a prompted LLM. The four outcomes (TP · TN · FP · FN), precision and recall, accuracy between two coders, and Cohen’s κ as agreement beyond chance — how much κ is enough, and quadratic weighted κ when labels are ordered.
C · The define-first workflow — you cannot evaluate what you have not defined. The five phases, borrowed from Eguchi & Kyle’s (2024) model-agnostic pipeline: ① define the annotation task, ② operationalize it into a scheme and guidelines, ③ build the gold standard, ④ set the target at human agreement, ⑤ evaluate the LLM against gold.
D · The dataset for the class tutorials — Arase, Uchida & Kajiwara (2022), the CEFR-SP corpus: 17k English sentences, each labelled with a CEFR level. One sentence in, one level out — familiar enough to be worth doing and small enough to finish in five days.
This is the conceptual grounding for the hands-on annotation in Session 5, which executes phases ①–③, and the evaluation code in Session 6, which executes phases ④–⑤.






Note



Before Session 5, skim §3.1 and §3.2 of Arase et al. (2022) — about a page and a half. The afternoon session opens by asking you to pull two design decisions out of it.

title: Session 6: Gold Standards & Evaluation Metrics
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Decide, for a single item, which of TP · FP · FN · TN it lands in, and write that decision as an if/elif.
Loop over a labelled set, store one verdict per item, and tally the four counts.
Build a confusion matrix from those counts and read it — which errors are misses, and which are false alarms.
Compute precision, recall, F1 and Cohen’s κ from scratch, and say what question each one answers.
Reproduce all of it with scikit-learn on the real six-level task — classification_report, confusion_matrix, cohen_kappa_score — and choose between plain and weighted κ depending on whether your labels are ordered.
Read a gold file as a {id, text, label} list of dicts, and recognise with open(...) for reading/writing data files.
Interpret the metrics critically — what a high or low score does and doesn’t tell you.

text:
Agenda
Yesterday’s question was “do two people agree?” Today’s is “is the model any good?” — the same tools, with one column swapped. Works through day2-s6_evaluation_metrics.ipynb in two passes over the same data.
Pass 1 — you build the metrics (notebook Part A). On a single yes/no question — is this sentence advanced? — so there are four counts to track instead of thirty-six, and twelve items you can count by hand.

Collapse six CEFR levels to one yes/no question, and name the positive class.
Decide one item with an if, then all four outcomes with an if/elif ladder.
Wrap it in a function, loop over the items, and store every verdict.
Tally the verdicts → build the confusion matrix → read it.
Derive precision, recall, F1 and Cohen’s κ from those same four numbers.
Re-run on all 72 items, then check your code against scikit-learn.

Pass 2 — scikit-learn at scale (notebook Part B). The real six-level task: classification_report as one-vs-rest run six times, the confusion matrix read down the columns, plain vs. quadratic-weighted κ, and error analysis — “is the disagreement the model’s fault, or the scheme’s?”
The session closes with the 作戦会議 strategy huddle: turn today’s mechanics onto your own project track — a draft annotation scheme, your gold source, and the agreement you would accept.
The whole session runs on frozen predictions — no API key, no live model — so everyone’s numbers come out identical every run. You’ll run the model live yourself from Day 3 onward; today the focus is measuring quality, not producing it.

title: Session 9: Error Analysis & Under-the-Hood Walkthrough
text:
Agenda

Error analysis — the number shows that something changed; the errors show why. Read down the per-class F1 column first, then separate the two causes: the model is wrong, or the scheme is fuzzy.
Iterating the prompt — say what you expect before you run it, then check the class you aimed at. One change per round.
Inside run_prompt — a walkthrough of the helper you have called all day: how it fills the {text} slot, paces the calls to stay under the rate limit, retries on a 429, scans the reply for the label, and returns labels in gold order. You do not edit it; the point is being able to describe what it does.
The LLM is one option, not the only one — put your score next to the published supervised results for the same corpus, and work out what that comparison does and does not license.

title: Session 9: Error Analysis & Under-the-Hood Walkthrough
text:
The CEFR wrap-up
You spent Day 3 pushing a prompt as far as it goes on CEFR levels. The closing question is the honest one: how good is that, really?
Arase, Uchida & Kajiwara (2022) — the paper behind the corpus you have been using since Session 4 — trained models on this exact task and reported them in their Table 6. Their test split is 3,012 sentences; ours is a balanced 72-item draw, so these are not the same measurement. But both are macro-F1 over the same six labels on the same corpus, which is enough to see where prompting sits:








System
macro-F1
Quadratic weighted κ




Bag-of-words + SVM (their naive baseline)
41.2
0.354


k-NN over frozen BERT embeddings
38.8
0.373


BERT-Base classifier, loss-weighted
82.5
0.609


Their proposed metric-based model
84.5
0.628


Our zero-shot prompt, Day 2 frozen run (72 items)
≈36
0.849



Two things to take from this, both uncomfortable in a useful way:

A zero-shot prompt lands near a bag-of-words baseline, not near a trained model. The gap to 84.5 is what a labelled training set buys — and CEFR-SP took trained experts to build. That is the cost side of the trade.
Our weighted κ looks better than theirs. It is not, and working out why is the exercise: our 72 items are balanced 12-per-level while their test set is not, and κ is sensitive to the marginal distribution. A number that flatters you across two different test sets is exactly the kind of comparison a reader should refuse — and the kind your own report must not make.

The point is not that prompting is bad. It is that “the model got 36” means nothing until you can say 36 compared to what, on which items.

Every number in that column is measured on dev. It is your steering wheel, not your result.

If you change two things and the score moves, you cannot tell which change caused it.

title: Session 13: Project Work — Prompt Iteration & Final Evaluation
text:
“Added examples” is not an explanation






Weak


“Round 1: added few-shot examples. F1 went up.”









Strong


“Round 0 confused B1 with B2 on 7 of 14 items. Round 1 added one example of each, chosen from the pool. B1 recall rose 0.29 → 0.57; the B1/B2 confusion halved.”



The second one shows that you read the confusion matrix. That is the skill being assessed.

title: Session 13: Project Work — Prompt Iteration & Final Evaluation
section: Use the matrix to choose the next change
text:
Use the matrix to choose the next change
evaluate(dev, pred0, ordered=True)     # dev — the half you are allowed to look at
Look at the off-diagonal cells, not only the macro-F1:

Most confused pair — which two labels?
Adjacent (B1↔︎B2) — a calibration problem on an ordered scale; often fixable with clearer definitions or anchor examples.
Distant (A1↔︎C2) — the model is reading the prompt differently from how you intended.

title: Session 13: Project Work — Prompt Iteration & Final Evaluation
text:
Plain vs. weighted κ
Cohen's kappa            0.200
Cohen's kappa (weighted) 0.871   <- labels are ordered
  scale order used: A1 < A2 < B1 < B2 < C1 < C2

A large difference like this means: the model is usually one level away, and rarely exactly correct.
That is a different finding from “the model performs badly”, and only weighted κ shows it.

title: Session 13: Project Work — Prompt Iteration & Final Evaluation
section: But only when the labels are a scale
text:
But only when the labels are a scale
ordered=True is right for A1 < A2 < … < C2 and Move 1 < 2 < 3.
It is wrong for error categories — Grammatical is not “closer to” Lexical than to Mechanical.






And watch the order


Low/Mid/High is ordered but not alphabetical. Pass it yourself:
evaluate(dev, pred, ordered=True, labels=["Low", "Mid", "High"])
Otherwise the scale is High < Low < Mid and the number cannot be interpreted. evaluate prints the order it used — read that line.

title: Session 13: Project Work — Prompt Iteration & Final Evaluation
text:
Commit first, then open it
Fill this in before the next cell runs:
CANDIDATES = {                                  # every prompt you will test
    "v1 few-shot": ROOT / "prompts" / (TRACK + ".txt"),
}
WINNER_RULE = "highest macro-F1; ties go to the simpler prompt"

You may test more than one prompt. That is legitimate — but it is a different claim from testing one, and the difference is entirely whether you said so in advance.

title: Session 13: Project Work — Prompt Iteration & Final Evaluation
text:
Then run it, once
test = load_gold(TEST_PATH)          # the first time this file is opened all week

freeze_test_run(load_prompt(CANDIDATES[name]), test, f1_by_round, ...)
freeze_test_run runs the prompt, saves before scoring anything, reads that file back off disk, scores those predictions, and appends one line to a log that travels in your submission.







Report every number you tested, not the best one


Three prompts tested and the best reported is the best of three tries, optimistic by an amount nobody can work out afterwards. All three go in report §3.

title: Session 13: Project Work — Prompt Iteration & Final Evaluation
section: Nothing stops you running it twice
text:
Nothing stops you running it twice
Stopping you would be the wrong design — a real mistake at four o’clock needs a way forward.
So instead nothing is overwritten: a second run lands in ..._predictions_attempt2.json beside the first, and both stay.

Every scoring appends a line to ..._test_log.jsonl, fingerprinted with the prompt that produced it. Same fingerprint twice = one prompt run twice. Different fingerprints = a prompt changed after seeing the held-out set — and report §5 has to say which happened.

title: Session 13: Project Work — Prompt Iteration & Final Evaluation
text:
One run, one person






Important


Runtimes are per-person. Your reported numbers must come from a single frozen file, so decide who runs the model before you start.



Free tier: ~500 calls/day per key. If that person reaches the daily limit during the session, another member takes over and runs the notebook in their own runtime. The files remain in your shared Drive folder.

That is one of the reasons the whole group works from one cloned folder.

text:

Yesterday’s question was “do two people agree?” Today’s is “is the model any good?” — same tools, one column swapped.

Pass 1 — you build the metrics. TP/FP/FN/TN → confusion matrix → precision, recall, F1 → Cohen’s κ. No libraries.
Pass 2 — scikit-learn does it at scale, on all six CEFR levels at once.
作戦会議 — turn today’s mechanics onto your own project track.

text:
Recap: the define-first workflow
S4 laid out five phases. S5 ran ③ — you built a gold standard. Today you evaluate a model against it.

① Define the task · ② Operationalize · ③ Build the gold standard (yesterday)
④ Target = human agreement ← the highest score you can realistically expect, set by your κ from S5
⑤ Evaluate the model against gold ← today








The same tool, one column swapped


In S5 you compared annotator A vs. annotator B → inter-annotator agreement. Today you compare gold vs. model → model evaluation. Identical formulas. Identical code. Only the second column changed.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
section: What you already know from S4
text:
What you already know from S4
You have already met all of today’s math. Today you implement it.


The four cells — rows = gold, columns = prediction




Pred +
Pred −




Gold +
TP
FN

The formulas
\[P = \frac{TP}{TP+FP} \qquad R = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\]
\[F_1 = 2\cdot\frac{P\cdot R}{P+R} \qquad \kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}\]


Knowing a formula and being able to compute it are different things. After today, you can explain how every number in your project was calculated.

text:
The same data, asked twice
We use the CEFR-SP set from S5: 72 sentences, 12 per level, and a model’s frozen predictions for each.









Pass 1 — you build it
Pass 2 — scikit-learn

“Is this sentence advanced?” (yes/no)

Cells to track
4

Tools

classification_report, confusion_matrix, cohen_kappa_score


You learn
where the numbers come from
how to get them at scale










Why binary first


Four cells are small enough to count by hand. Everything you build in pass 1 is exactly what scikit-learn does in pass 2 — six times, once per level.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Today runs on frozen predictions
No API key, no live model. The model was run once, offline, and its answers committed to a file.

Day 1 — you saw the model’s answers change from run to run.
Problem — that variation makes it impossible to tell a coding mistake from a model difference.
So today — everyone’s precision, recall, F1 and κ are identical. If your number differs from the slide, you have a bug in your code.

You run the model yourself, live, from Day 3 on.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Load the data first
Every evaluation begins by loading the two things it compares — the gold standard and the model’s predictions. This is a step of its own; the confusion matrix later is built from exactly what you load here.
gold = load_gold(GOLD_URL)                        # 72 records: {id, text, label}
predictions = load_predictions(PREDICTIONS_URL)   # one level per item, same order

Both are plain lists in the same order: predictions[i] is the model’s answer for gold[i].

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Six levels → one question
CEFR has six levels. For pass 1 we ask one thing:

Is this sentence advanced — C1 or C2?


"yes" = C1 or C2 → this is our positive class
"no" = A1, A2, B1, B2








Note


Choosing the positive class is a decision, not a technicality. “Precision” and “recall” are always about the positive class. Change what counts as positive and every number changes. In your project, say out loud which class is positive before you report a score.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
section: Build the twelve from what you loaded
text:
Build the twelve from what you loaded
The twelve rows are not typed in — they are sliced from the gold and predictions you just loaded (ids 17–28) and collapsed to yes/no. Same for, if, dictionaries as the rest of pass 1:
ADVANCED = ["C1", "C2"]          # the levels that count as "yes"

gold_12 = gold[16:28]            # positions 16–27 → ids 17–28
pred_12 = predictions[16:28]

items = []
i = 0
for g in gold_12:
    p = pred_12[i]               # the model's answer for that same sentence
    if g["label"] in ADVANCED:
        gold_answer = "yes"
    else:
        gold_answer = "no"
    if p in ADVANCED:
        pred_answer = "yes"
    else:
        pred_answer = "no"
    items.append({"id": g["id"], "text": g["text"],
                  "gold": gold_answer, "pred": pred_answer})
    i = i + 1

Ask it the first question
Is this item a true positive? That means both labels are "yes":

An if with no else prints nothing when the condition is false. To classify every item we need all four questions, and exactly one of them must run.

Four cells, four branches, in the same order.

    print("TP")      # advanced, and the model said advanced

Why store them, rather than just count?
We could have counted as we went. We keep the list because the list records every individual decision.

A metric is a summary. decisions is what is being summarised, and you can always return to it.
Each 'FN' and 'FP' points to a specific sentence you can read and discuss.
That is error analysis — the source of your research questions: is this the model’s error, or a problem in my scheme?

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
section: Precision — of what it called advanced, how much was correct?
text:
Precision — of what it called advanced, how much was correct?
Numbers first, so you can check it on paper:
print(3 / (3 + 1))            # TP / (TP + FP)
0.75

Same thing, read off the tally — so it survives a change of data:
print(tally["TP"] / (tally["TP"] + tally["FP"]))    # the same, from the tally
0.75


Of the 4 sentences the model called advanced, 3 really were. Precision = 0.75.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Precision — now as a function
def precision(tally):
    """Of everything CALLED advanced, how much really was?  TP / (TP + FP)"""
    tp = tally.get("TP", 0)      # .get(..., 0) so a missing count reads as 0
    fp = tally.get("FP", 0)
    if tp + fp == 0:             # the model never said "yes" at all
        return 0.0               # no correct positives, and no division by zero
    return tp / (tp + fp)        # correct positives, over all positive predictions

print(round(precision(tally), 3))   # round to 3 decimal places

0.75








Always guard the denominator


If a model never predicts the positive class, TP + FP is 0 and Python raises ZeroDivisionError. Returning 0.0 records that there were no correct positive predictions. Every metric you write today needs this guard.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Recall — your turn
Recall asks the other question: of everything that truly was advanced, how much did we identify?
\[R = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\]
def recall(tally):
    """Of everything that TRULY was advanced, how much did we identify?"""
    tp = tally.get("TP", 0)
    fn = tally.get("FN", 0)       # ← the only real change
    if tp + fn == 0:              # nothing was truly advanced, so there is nothing to find
        return 0.0
    return tp / (tp + fn)         # correct positives, over all true positives in the gold

print(round(recall(tally), 3))

0.6
Three of the five genuinely advanced sentences were found. Recall = 0.60.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
section: F1 — precision and recall in one number
text:
F1 — precision and recall in one number
Precision and recall move in opposite directions: if the model labels everything positive, recall becomes 1.0 and precision becomes very low. F1 is the harmonic mean, so a high value on one side cannot compensate for a low value on the other:
\[F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{P \cdot R}{P + R}\]
def f1(tally):
    """Harmonic mean of precision and recall."""
    p = precision(tally)         # reuse the function you just wrote
    r = recall(tally)            # ...and the other one
    if p + r == 0:               # both zero — nothing to average
        return 0.0
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r)   # harmonic mean: a low value on either side lowers it

print(round(precision(tally), 3), round(recall(tally), 3), round(f1(tally), 3))

0.75 0.6 0.667

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
What 0.75 vs. 0.60 actually says
The gap between precision and recall describes how the model behaves:

Precision 0.75 > Recall 0.60 — the model applies the label advanced less often than the gold data does. When it does apply it, it is usually correct, but it labels some real C1 sentences as B2.
Both errors were C1 → B2 (rows 22, 24) — one level away, not far away.








Which error matters more in your project?


That is a research design question, not a statistics one.

Selecting texts for a C1 reading list — an FN (an advanced sentence you do not find) is more serious; favour recall.
Claiming in a paper which sentences are advanced — an FP (a sentence wrongly called advanced) is more serious; favour precision.

Say which one your project cares about before you report a score.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Why accuracy isn’t enough
Start with the easy number — observed agreement, the diagonal over the total:
n = tally["TP"] + tally["FP"] + tally["FN"] + tally["TN"]   # all 12 items
p_o = (tally["TP"] + tally["TN"]) / n   # the diagonal (both agreed), over the total
print(round(p_o, 3))

0.75


Gold and model agree on 9 of 12 items. That looks acceptable — but a model that answered “no” to every item would score 7/12 without using any information at all. Raw agreement gives a high score to a model that simply predicts the most frequent label.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Agreement expected by chance
\(p_e\) = the agreement two raters would reach by chance, given how often each one uses each label. Multiply their rates, label by label — the row and column totals from step 7:
# each line: how often GOLD says it × how often the MODEL says it = chance agreement
p_yes = ((tally["TP"] + tally["FN"]) / n) * ((tally["TP"] + tally["FP"]) / n)
p_no  = ((tally["FP"] + tally["TN"]) / n) * ((tally["FN"] + tally["TN"]) / n)
p_e   = p_yes + p_no          # chance agreement on "yes" plus chance agreement on "no"
print(round(p_yes, 3), round(p_no, 3), round(p_e, 3))

0.139 0.389 0.528



p_yes: gold says yes 5/12 × model says yes 4/12 = 0.139
p_no: gold says no 7/12 × model says no 8/12 = 0.389
More than half the agreement we observed (0.75) is expected by chance alone.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
κ — agreement corrected for chance
\[\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}\]
Of the agreement that chance does not explain, how much did they achieve?
# observed minus chance agreement (p_o - p_e), over the agreement still available (1 - p_e):
print(round((p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e), 3))

0.471







Cohen’s κ
Landis & Koch
McHugh




0.21–0.40
Fair
Minimal


0.41–0.60
Moderate
Weak


0.61–0.80
Substantial
Moderate




75% agreement → κ = 0.47.
The same gap S4 showed you (80% → κ ≈ 0.52), now computed by your own code.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
section: The whole calculation as one function
text:
The whole calculation as one function
def kappa(tally):
    """Agreement corrected for chance: (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)."""
    n = tally["TP"] + tally["FP"] + tally["FN"] + tally["TN"]   # every item
    p_o = (tally["TP"] + tally["TN"]) / n     # agreement we actually observed
    p_yes = ((tally["TP"] + tally["FN"]) / n) * ((tally["TP"] + tally["FP"]) / n)
    p_no = ((tally["FP"] + tally["TN"]) / n) * ((tally["FN"] + tally["TN"]) / n)
    p_e = p_yes + p_no                        # agreement expected by chance
    if 1 - p_e == 0:                          # chance already explains all agreement
        return 0.0
    return (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)            # the share of the remaining agreement achieved







This is yesterday’s function


Nothing in kappa() knows whether column two came from your partner or a model. That is why S5’s agreement number and today’s evaluation number are the same statistic: κ measures two label columns, whoever produced them.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
section: Does your code match the library?
text:
Does your code match the library?
You built a confusion matrix and four metrics by hand. Before trusting them, check them against scikit-learn on the same twelve items — it builds the same 2×2 and computes the same numbers, and if yours differ you have a bug. This is the only place scikit-learn enters pass 1:
✅ TP/FP/FN/TN     yours=3/1/2/6  sklearn=3/1/2/6
✅ precision      yours=0.750000  sklearn=0.750000
✅ recall         yours=0.600000  sklearn=0.600000
✅ f1             yours=0.666667  sklearn=0.666667
✅ cohen_kappa    yours=0.470588  sklearn=0.470588
-----------------------------------------------
All 5 checks passed ✅  — your confusion matrix and metrics match scikit-learn.







This is the point of pass 1


sklearn is not doing anything you cannot do. It is doing exactly what you just wrote, faster and for every class at once. Twelve items is enough to learn the mechanics, never enough to judge a model — so pass 2 hands the full 72 to scikit-learn. From here on, when a report prints 0.36, you know precisely which counts produced it.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Six levels, thirty-six cells
Drop the yes/no simplification. The actual task is the full ordinal CEFR scale: A1 · A2 · B1 · B2 · C1 · C2. Nothing new is loaded — the gold and predictions from the start already carry the full level; pass 1 only collapsed them to yes/no.

4 cells → 36. Counting by hand is no longer practical.
One positive class at a time — with six classes you get six precisions, six recalls, six F1s.
The method is unchanged — to score C1, treat C1 as “yes” and all five others as “no”: pass 1, run six times. This is called one-vs-rest, and it is what classification_report does.


# The gold labels as a plain list — the shape every scikit-learn call wants:
y_true = []
for item in gold:
    y_true.append(item["label"])
y_pred = predictions              # the model's labels, already a plain list

print(classification_report(y_true, y_pred, labels=LEVELS, zero_division=0))
These are the names from the table in pass 1, called directly. You built each one by hand — this is the same work, for six classes at once.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
section: Accuracy is 39% — now look at how it is wrong
text:
Accuracy is 39% — now look at how it is wrong
Before concluding that the model is useless, look at the size of its errors.


97% of its answers are within one level of the gold label.
Only two sentences in the whole set are two levels away. No answer is further than that.
A model that had not learned the task would predict C2 for A1 sentences. This one does not.









Important


“Right idea, imprecise thresholds” is a completely different failure from “doesn’t understand the task” — and no single accuracy number can tell them apart. That is what the confusion matrix is for.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Central-tendency bias
The model said A2 twenty times and A1 four times. It said C2 exactly once — in 72 chances.


Predictions concentrate in the middle of the scale; the two ends are used rarely.
Why? When a rater — human or machine — has to judge something as unclear as “difficulty”, the middle categories are the safest choice.
Same finding as pass 1 — with “advanced” as positive, precision ran ahead of recall (0.75 vs 0.60 on your twelve). The model under-uses the top of the scale.









Tip


You will meet this tendency in your own annotation — and in your teammates’. It is one of the first things to check in a scheme that isn’t reaching acceptable κ.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Two κ values, same data
weights="quadratic" is the one argument that separates them:
print("Cohen's kappa           ", round(cohen_kappa_score(y_true, y_pred), 3))

# weights="quadratic": A1 -> A2 is a smaller error than A1 -> C2.
weighted = cohen_kappa_score(y_true, y_pred, labels=LEVELS, weights="quadratic")
print("Cohen's kappa (weighted)", round(weighted, 3), "  <- labels are ordered")
Cohen's kappa            0.267
Cohen's kappa (weighted) 0.849   <- labels are ordered

Plain κ = 0.27 (“fair” / “minimal”) — because plain κ treats A1 → A2 as exactly as wrong as A1 → C2.
Quadratic-weighted κ = 0.85 — because CEFR levels are ordinal, so an error of one level should count less than an error of five:
\[w_{ij} = \frac{(i-j)^2}{(N-1)^2}\]








Report the one that matches your labels


Same predictions, 0.27 or 0.85 depending on a single argument. Ordered labels → weighted κ. Unordered categories → plain κ. State which you used and why; a κ reported without that sentence cannot be interpreted. (Arase et al. reported weighted κ = .628 on this task.)

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
section: Error analysis — the model’s error, or the scheme’s?
text:
Error analysis — the model’s error, or the scheme’s?
rows = []
for g, p in zip(gold, predictions):   # walk gold and predictions side by side
    if g["label"] != p:               # keep only the disagreements
        rows.append({"id": g["id"], "gold": g["label"], "pred": p, "text": g["text"]})
print(len(rows), "of", len(gold), "wrong.")

errors = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["id", "gold", "pred", "text"])
errors.head(15)     # ...or errors[errors["gold"] == "C2"] for the highest level
44 errors — too many to read one by one, and you do not need to. Read about a dozen, then look closely at the rows where gold is C2 or A1: disagreements concentrate at the two ends of the scale.

For each error you read, ask:

Is the gold defensible here, or is this genuinely borderline?
Would you and your partner have agreed on this sentence?
Would a better-written scheme have prevented this error?









Note


Remember rows 19, 23 and 25 — the three obituary sentences. In pass 1’s yes/no task the model got all three right. In six classes it labelled every one of them A2 instead of A1. The question you ask determines which errors you can see.

title: Session 6: Evaluation Metrics
section: Apply today’s session to your own project
text:
Apply today’s session to your own project
Everything this week has used CEFR-SP. Your project uses different data. Spend the next ~12 minutes with your team adding three things to your 作戦シート:

A draft annotation scheme — your label set, plus one line of guideline per label. (Steps ①②.)
Your gold source — the provided pool, or one you build yourselves? Who annotates, and how many items? (Step ③.)
The agreement you would accept — a κ number, decided now, before you see any results. Also state which class is positive, and whether your labels are ordered (→ weighted κ) or not.








Tip


Teams often skip point 3. A threshold chosen after seeing the number is not a threshold; it is a justification written afterwards.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
🎯 Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Describe an annotation task as labels placed on a unit of analysis, and say why applied-linguistic findings depend on it.
Explain why this course targets sentence and text categorization, and what changes for span-level tasks.

Explain inter-annotator agreement: percent agreement vs. why Cohen’s κ corrects for chance — including quadratic weighted κ for ordered labels.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
What is annotation?
Annotation = adding interpretive labels to the available linguistic data.

POS — noun / verb / adjective…
Word sense — which meaning of bank?
Stance / engagement — is the writer hedging, endorsing?
Discourse moves — what is this sentence doing in the argument?
Error tags, …, CEFR level,

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Annotation
Annotation: Putting labels on a specific unit of analysis

Label:

The actual value (often category) we put as a result of the annotation

Unit of analysis:

The chunk/layer that the specific annotation will be put on.

Morphology
Word
Multiword Units
Sentence
Paragraph …

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Part of Speech
POS tagging = label every token with its grammatical category (NOUN, VERB, ADJ…). One label per token — the simplest sequence-labelling task.
The_DET dogs_NOUN ran_VERB quickly_ADV ._PUNCT

Penn Tag

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Word Sense Disambiguation
Word-sense disambiguation = decide which meaning a word carries in context. Same form, different sense.

She sat on the bank of the river. → riverbank
She deposited the cheque at the bank. → financial institution

The surface form is identical — only context resolves the sense. Harder than POS: the label set is per word, not a fixed grammar.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement

Syntactic Dependency
Dependency parsing = Identifying a binary syntactic relationships between a head and its dependency.

Dependency tree for “They buy and sell books.”

Stance


Stance annotation = label how a writer positions themselves toward a proposition .
Unit of analysis is a span - textual segments with specified beginning and end.

The four outcomes: TP · TN · FP · FN
First pick one class as positive — say, “this sentence hedges.” Every prediction then belongs to one of four cells. Rows = gold (the truth), columns = the prediction:

Precision & Recall
Two questions about the positive class, from the same four cells. Say our detector scored the following on a batch of sentences:




Pred +
Pred −

TP = 8

Precision — of everything it labelled positive, how much was correct?
Recall — of everything that was actually positive, how much did it identify?

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Precision & Recall
Precision — of everything it labelled positive, how much was correct?
\[\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{8}{8 + 2} = 0.80\]
Recall — of everything that was actually positive, how much did it identify?
\[\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{8}{8 + 4} = 0.67\]
F1 — the harmonic mean, so a high value on one side cannot compensate for a low value on the other:
\[F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{P \cdot R}{P + R} = 2 \cdot \frac{0.80 \cdot 0.67}{0.80 + 0.67} \approx 0.73\]

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Cohen’s κ — agreement beyond chance
Cohen’s κ (the two-rater, nominal case) subtracts the agreement you’d expect by chance:
\[\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}\] \(p_e\) = the agreement they would reach by chance, using each coder’s own marginal rate (row/column totals ÷ 50).

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Cohen’s κ — agreement beyond chance
For each label, multiply the two coders’ rates:
\[p_e = \underbrace{P(A{+})\cdot P(B{+})}_{\text{both say }+} \;+\; \underbrace{P(A{-})\cdot P(B{-})}_{\text{both say }-}\]
Here both coders marked “+” 15/50 = 0.30 and “−” 35/50 = 0.70:
\[p_e = (0.30)(0.30) + (0.70)(0.70) = 0.58 \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \kappa = \frac{0.80 - 0.58}{1 - 0.58} \approx 0.52\]

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
How much κ is enough?
There’s no single cut-off — you read κ against a benchmark.



Cohen’s κ
Landis & Koch (1977)
McHugh (2012)




< 0.00
Poor
—


0.00–0.20
Slight
None


0.21–0.40
Fair

0.41–0.60

0.61–0.80

0.81–1.00

Strong









Tip


Our two coders’ raw 80 % agreement is only κ ≈ 0.52 once chance is removed — inadequate on that rule. This difference is why κ is reported instead of raw agreement.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Ordered labels: quadratic weighted κ
Plain κ treats every disagreement as equally bad — scoring A1 → A2 exactly as wrong as A1 → C2. But CEFR levels are ordinal (A1 < A2 < … < C2), so an error of one level should count less than an error of five.
Weighted κ puts a penalty \(w_{ij}\) on each off-diagonal cell. With quadratic weights over \(N\) ordered levels (indices \(i, j\)):
\[w_{ij} = \frac{(i - j)^2}{(N - 1)^2}, \qquad \kappa_w = 1 - \frac{\sum_{ij} w_{ij}\,O_{ij}}{\sum_{ij} w_{ij}\,E_{ij}}\]
For CEFR (\(N = 6\)): an error of one level weighs \(\tfrac{1}{25} = 0.04\) (barely penalized); a distant A1 ↔︎ C2 error weighs \(\tfrac{25}{25} = 1.0\) (full penalty).

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
Why define the task first?
An LLM’s P / R / F1 is only meaningful against a gold standard — and a gold standard only exists once the category is operationalized well enough that two coders agree beyond chance.

No gold → the score has nothing to compare against.
Fuzzy category → coders disagree → no trustworthy gold in the first place.

So before we prompt anything, we define the task well enough that humans can agree on it.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
The loop we borrow — model-agnostic
Eguchi & Kyle (2024) lay out an 11-step tool-building pipeline.
It runs define → operationalize → gold → evaluate — the model comes almost last:

The steps that define the task and judge the output don’t care what produces the labels.
So we keep them and swap their trained model for a prompted LLM.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
① Define the annotation task

Scope & purpose — What is the source text?
Design the task — input → output over a unit of analysis of choice.
Reuse or draft — adopt an existing scheme / tag set if one fits; else draft from the literature.
Choose the metrics now (P / R / F1, κ) — so evaluation is planned, not retrofitted.
Sample data to represent the domain (proficiency, L1) and fix the unit.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
section: ② Operationalize into a scheme + guidelines
text:
② Operationalize into a scheme + guidelines

Turn the theoretical construct into descriptive rules.

Fuoli (2018) gives three principles:

All choices accounted for.
Guidelines tested & refined until reliable.
Reliability always assessed — and reported.

If two trained coders can’t agree on it, a model can’t be trusted on it either.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
text:
③ Build the gold standard

Two coders annotate the same items blind.
Measure inter-annotator agreement — percent + κ.
Read the confusion matrix → refine the scheme, re-annotate.
Adjudicate disagreements → a gold standard.

title: Session 4: Annotation Principles & Inter-Annotator Agreement
section: ④ Set the target = human agreement
text:
④ Set the target = human agreement
(E&K Step 8a) — the highest score you can realistically expect from any model is the human IAA.

E&K expected ~0.70 F1 because their coders agreed at ~0.67 κ.







Note


The central point: the better you define the task, the higher humans agree — and the more you can legitimately ask of the LLM.

The 作戦シート, now as a file in your repo
You have been building this plan since S3 — track, scheme, gold source, prompting strategy. Today it becomes a file in your repo, and it grows three questions the notebooks deliberately do not ask you.
It is not graded. It is a required step: no group calls the model until it is signed.

Two minutes of writing prevents problems that otherwise take an hour to find, after you have used your quota:

label set says Move 1/2/3, gold file says 1a/1b, prompt says “move one” → no error, just a confusing F1
labels ordered but not alphabetical → weighted κ computed over High < Low < Mid
nobody agreed who codes which column → one annotator, no κ
the statistic picked after seeing which one came out higher → a number nobody can check

text:
Nine questions
What you are annotating:
1. Unit of analysis: sentence or whole text — and why
2. Label set: exactly the strings in your gold file
3. Are the labels ORDERED? In what order?  → labels_order
4. The ✏️ decisions you made building the pool, and what they cost
5. Sampling: which strategy, and the one-sentence defence
6. The dev / test split — and why that ratio
What you will report — and this is the half that is new:
7. QC: who codes what · WHICH agreement statistics, and why
      · what counts as a disagreement
8. Prompt plan: the moves, in order · how many prompts you will
      test on the held-out set · how you pick the winner
9. The ONE number you lead with: macro / micro / weighted F1, or κ

title: Session 11: Plenary Pipeline Assembly
section: Why 7–9 are on this page and not in a notebook
text:
Why 7–9 are on this page and not in a notebook
Every one of them decides a number you will report — and every one has an answer you could reach for after seeing which option flatters you.

Nothing stops you running all three F1 averages and reporting the highest. No reader of your report could tell.








The rule


Looking is fine when it changes what you do next. It is not fine when it changes what you claim.
Reading the coder confusion matrix to decide which boundary to argue about is exactly what it is for. Choosing the statistic after seeing what each one gives you is not.

section: Before LLM — Brief history of embedding
text:
Before LLM — Brief history of embedding
LLM encodes language into numbers — i.e., embedding.
Embedding: “vector representations of the meaning of words that are learned directly from word distributions in texts” (Jurafsky & Martin, 2026, p. 96).
Two families, and we build up to both:

Static — one fixed vector per word: counting contexts, then Word2Vec.
Contextual — a different vector each time the word appears: BERT, and the models you use.

title: Session 1: Introduction to LLMs as Tools for Linguistic Data Analysis
text:
RGB color space
A vector is a list of numbers that fixes the location of something in a space. A colour, for example, is fixed by how much red, green and blue it has.
Move the sliders to change the colour. Drag the cube to rotate it.

The dashed path is the vector: R along red, then G along green, then B along blue. The number under each name is the distance from your colour to that colour — close in the space = similar colour. Word embeddings work the same way, with hundreds of numbers instead of three.

section: word2vec: We actually do not need a table
text:
word2vec: We actually do not need a table

LSA support distributional semantics.

BUT LSA has some limitations:

LSA is usually applied to document-level co-occurrence, but a document can have multiple topics.
The table is huge and difficult to use large corpus.

→ We want to model the dimension without huge co-occurrence table and focusing on local co-occurence.

word2vec: Learns whether a word pair co-occur or not

...  your  [ account   is   free   of   charge ]  a  standard  fee ...

Arrow thickness is the weight the model gives that neighbour. Weights are illustrative.


Query — sent by bank, the word being built: which words here tell me what I mean?
Key — every other word’s answer. pond matches the query closely, the and walked do not, so pond gets a large weight.
Value — what each word contributes to the total.
Vector — the values added up, each multiplied by its weight. In the second sentence the same query meets different keys, so deposited and cheque take the weight and the sum comes out different.

section: Transformer make full use of attention
text:
Transformer make full use of attention


BERT-base models 12 layers of 12 attention heads.
GPT-3 had 96 layer × 96 heads = 9216 attention heads

title: Session 1: Introduction to LLMs as Tools for Linguistic Data Analysis
section: What an LLM lets you do
text:
What an LLM lets you do

It can label categories that depend on context. Most of the categories linguists work with are of that kind, and a bag-of-words model could never represent them.
One model, many tasks. Generative model can do many things with a prompt. We do not train a new model for each task with a new annotated training set.
Quick iteration: Annotation is painstaking, but you can iterate with LLM early.

title: Session 1: Introduction to LLMs as Tools for Linguistic Data Analysis
section: Sounding right is not being right
text:
Sounding right is not being right
An LLM essentially learns to predict next plausible word.
Plausible is not the same as correct — which is exactly what Curry et al. found when the output read well and the analysis was wrong.
That’s why we still need NLP evaluation.

title: Session 1: Introduction to LLMs as Tools for Linguistic Data Analysis
section: What people have already done with LLMs
text:
What people have already done with LLMs
Historically each task had its own model — a POS tagger, an NER model, a parser.
Already tons of research uses LLMs:








Study
What it annotated

AutoErrorAnalyzer

ICNALE GRA



Three of these are on your mini-project list. You can pick one as a group to work on conceptual replication.

title: Session 1: Introduction to LLMs as Tools for Linguistic Data Analysis
text:
What this course covers






Important


This course is the evaluation half of NLP, applied to LLMs.



We do not cover the training part of NLP. The evaluation part provides exactly the rigour an LLM’s outputs need, and that is what you will learn to run this week.

inter-annotator agreement (percent + Cohen’s κ)
precision / recall / F1, confusion matrix

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
📋 Agenda

Colab basics — run a cell, read an error
Your first LLM call — five prompts, and what they show
f-strings — put your data into the prompt
What the model returns — data types
Turn the answer into a record you can score
Getting the answers back out — indexing and slicing

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
🎯 Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Sign in to Colab, run a cell (Shift+Enter), and read a Python error well enough to fix a typo.
Store a value in a variable, and send a prompt with ai.generate_text(...).
Build a prompt from a variable with an f-string, and recognise the .format() template form.
Recognise str / list / dict in what the model returns.
Build the {id, text, label} record the rest of the course uses — with a label you decided yourself — and add the model’s answer beside it.
Index and slice into a list of records to compare the two answers.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
How today works

Slides give the idea for each step (a minute or two).
Then you do it in Colab — right away, while it’s fresh.

Two kinds of Colab moment:

👀 Let’s follow — run the cell together and watch what happens.
🧪 Let’s try — your turn: change something and re-run.







Tip


Errors are normal and expected today. Reading them is a skill we practise, not a sign anything is broken.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
Before we begin
Why do we learn Python syntax when LLM can write for us?

The role is changing; human conceptualize and supervise.
AI cannot take responsibility of your work.
Review is still your job; reading and being able to explain what is happening is critical.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
What Colab is
Colab = an online Python notebook Google offers (run code without installing anything).
A notebook = a document of cells you run one at a time.

Text cells (like this slide) — notes.
Code cells — Python that runs on a runtime (a free computer Google lends you in the cloud).
Run a cell with Shift + Enter.

Nothing installs on your laptop. If the runtime disconnects, you just re-run the cells.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
Why this matters
This is the workspace you’ll use for every work — every session runs here.
You will see red error messages. An error message is not a failure: it states which instruction Python could not carry out. Read the last line to find out what to fix.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
👀 Let’s follow — in Colab
Run your first cell:
print("Hello, Colab! You just ran your first cell.")

Now break it on purpose — a typo — and run it:
print(mesage)      # 'mesage' was never defined
Read the last line of the red box:
NameError: name 'mesage' is not defined
→ error type · message · line number.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
🧪 Let’s try — in Colab
Your turn:

print(...) a message of your own.
Then misspell a word or variable on purpose and read the error you get.
Fix it and re-run.

Reading that last line is the skill to practise here. You will use it all week.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
First — what’s a variable?
A variable is a name that stores a value.
level = "A1"        # store the text "A1" under the name `level`
print(level)        # get it back by name

name = value — the = means “store this”, not “equals”.
Once stored, reuse the value anywhere just by writing its name.


Next we store the model’s reply under the name reply.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
section: The basic operation, in one line
text:
The basic operation, in one line
You send the model text (a prompt); it sends text back (a reply).
reply = ai.generate_text("...your prompt...")


ai.generate_text(...) does the call — ai is Colab’s built-in Gemini, no API key today.
reply = ... stores the answer in a variable named reply, so you can use it later.



One call = one answer. That reply is not correct by definition; it is data you have to check. In Session 6 you will score answers like this against a human gold standard.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
Why this matters
This one call is the basis of everything this week.

Classification, annotation and evaluation are all variations on it: build a prompt, send it, read the reply. Once you can do this, the rest of the course changes the text around this call.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
👀 Let’s follow — in Colab
Run the 📦 Setup cell first, then run this together:
# ✏️ change the text in the quotes, then press Shift+Enter to re-run.
reply = ai.generate_text("In one sentence, what is applied linguistics?")
print(reply)                                    # show what came back
The model’s answer prints out. You just called an LLM from Python.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
🧪 Let’s try — in Colab
Your turn — change the prompt and re-run (a different topic, or another language):
reply = ai.generate_text("In one sentence, what is a corpus?")
print(reply)
The code is the same and the answer is different. The prompt is text that you control.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
section: Putting your data into the prompt
text:
Putting your data into the prompt
An f-string is a normal string with an f in front — anything in { } gets swapped for its value:
sentence = "Nevertheless, the findings were inconclusive."
prompt = f"What CEFR level (A1-C2) is this sentence? {sentence}"

{sentence} is replaced by the actual sentence text inside the prompt. You do not copy and paste, and you do not join strings manually.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
Why this matters
The prompt is now built from a variable.

Change the value of sentence and the prompt changes automatically. This is how you run one prompt over many sentences, which Session 3 turns into a loop.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
👀 Let’s follow — in Colab
Run this together — build a prompt from a variable, then send it:
sentence = "Nevertheless, the findings were inconclusive."   # ✏️ your sentence
prompt = f"What CEFR level (A1-C2) is this sentence? {sentence}"  # f = fill in {}
print("Prompt sent:", prompt)                # see what {sentence} became

reply = ai.generate_text(prompt)             # send the finished prompt
print("Model says:", reply)

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
🧪 Let’s try — in Colab
Change sentence to one of your own and re-run.

You built a prompt from data and sent it. Every later session uses this same operation.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
The other form — a template
Without the f, the braces stay empty until something fills them:
TEMPLATE = """What CEFR level (A1-C2) is this sentence?
Answer with just the level.

Sentence: {text}"""

print(TEMPLATE.format(text="The cat sat on the mat."))   # .format() fills {text}


Three quotes ("""...""") hold a prompt written over several lines.
.format() fills the slot — one sentence at a time.

From Session 7 you edit templates like this, so recognise the shape. In the notebook you write one yourself.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
section: Python labels every value with a type
text:
Python labels every value with a type
The reply is still in reply. Before you can do anything with it, you have to know what kind of value it is.
print(reply)              # the model's answer, still in the variable from step 5
print(type(reply))        # <class 'str'> — a string, i.e. text
print(len(reply))         # how many characters of text that is
The three types you need all week:

str — text, in quotes: "A1".
list — many items in order, in brackets: ["a", "b", "c"].
dict — a labelled record, in braces: {"label": "A1"} (key → value).

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
A few more types
Here are some more frequent variable types.

int — whole numbers: 42
float — decimals: 3.14
bool — True / False
tuple — like a list, but its contents cannot be changed: (1, 2)
None — “nothing here yet”

You do not need to memorise these. When you see one, you will recognise it as another kind of value.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
🧪 Let’s try — predict first
Write down what you expect each line to print, then run it. Two of the four surprise most people.
print(len("A1"))                   # how long is the text "A1"?
print(type("A1") == type(reply))   # is a level the same type as a whole reply?
print(type(7))                     # a number
print(type("7"))                   # the same digit, in quotes

"A1" and a three-paragraph reply are the same type — str says what kind of value, not how much. And 7 and "7" differ: one you can divide, one is text.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
section: A label is a decision, not a computation
text:
A label is a decision, not a computation
A string is one thing. To ask whether the model is any good, you need two answers side by side:

what a person said the level is, and
what the model said.








Important


The label in a gold standard is a decision a person made. That is what you and your group spend Day 2 doing, by hand. A program does not produce it.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
👀 Let’s follow — your judgment first
Read the sentence, decide its level yourself, then build the record:
# ✏️ A1 is the simplest level, C2 the most advanced. Change it if you disagree.
text = "The cat sat on the mat."
my_level = "A1"

record = {"id": 1, "text": text, "label": my_level}   # a dict: named slots
print(record)                    # the whole record — note the { key: value ... }

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
section: 👀 Let’s follow — now ask the model
text:
👀 Let’s follow — now ask the model
Same sentence, same question, stored under a new key:
answer = ai.generate_text(f"What CEFR level (A1-C2) is this sentence? Answer with just the level. {text}")
record["model"] = answer.strip()   # .strip() drops the newline the reply arrives with
print(record)                      # the same record, now with two answers in it

record["model"] = ... — the same square brackets, now on the left of the =: that stores a value instead of reading one.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
One record, then many
A dataset is a list of records. Here are two more, already answered:
items = [record,                                              # the one you just built
         {"id": 2, "text": "More research is needed.",
          "label": "B1", "model": "B1"},
         {"id": 3, "text": "Nevertheless, the findings were inconclusive.",
          "label": "C1", "model": "B2"}]      # here the two answers disagree

print("how many items:", len(items))   # len() on a list = how many records
print(items[2])                        # the third record — counting starts at 0

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
section: 🧪 Let’s try — do you agree with it?
text:
🧪 Let’s try — do you agree with it?
Your own sentence, your own judgment. Write your level down before you run it.
my_text = "..."                       # ✏️ a sentence of your own
my_record = {"id": 4, "text": my_text, "label": "..."}   # ✏️ your judgment

prompt = f"What CEFR level (A1-C2) is this sentence? Answer with just the level. {my_text}"
my_record["model"] = ai.generate_text(prompt).strip()

print(my_record)
print("we agree:", my_record["label"] == my_record["model"])

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
Why this matters
{id, text, label} is the shape of every dataset in this course — the gold standard you build on Day 2, the file you score in Session 6, the sample you draw on Day 4.

The extra model key is what a prediction looks like once you have run one. Scoring is comparing those two columns.

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
Getting one item out
Use [...] to get one item:

a list by position (starts at 0): items[0]
a dict by key: record["label"]

Chain them to reach inside a record in a list: items[2]["label"].

title: Session 2: Colab Onboarding & Your First LLM Call
text:
👀 Let’s follow — in Colab
print("sentence 3:", items[2]["text"])    # list by position, then dict by key
print("person said:", items[2]["label"])
print("model said: ", items[2]["model"])
print("they agree: ", items[2]["label"] == items[2]["model"])   # == asks "same value?"

False — one record, one disagreement. On Day 2 you do this for every record and count the Trues. That count over the total is the first score you report.
