title: AutoErrorAnalyzer — download & preprocess
section: Step 5 — Build a balanced gold set
text:
Step 5 — Build a balanced gold set
Four classes × 15 = 60 items.


Show code
# Build a small BALANCED gold set: an equal number of items per label.
# Balance matters so precision/recall/F1 and the confusion matrix are meaningful.
import random
from collections import defaultdict

### Step 5.1: the two settings you control ###
PER_LABEL = 15          # how many items per label
random.seed(42)         # fixed seed = same sample every run (reproducible)

### Step 5.2: sort every reshaped row into a bucket named after its label ###
by_label = defaultdict(list)   # a dict that starts each new key at []
for item in rows:
    by_label[item["label"]].append(item)   # drop it in its label's bucket

### Step 5.3: shuffle each bucket, then take the first PER_LABEL from it ###
gold = []
for label in sorted(by_label):     # sorted() = same label order every run
    bucket = by_label[label]
    random.shuffle(bucket)         # mix, so we don't just take the first ones found
    gold.extend(bucket[:PER_LABEL])   # a rare label simply gives fewer

### Step 5.4: mix the labels together, renumber the ids from 1, and report ###
random.shuffle(gold)               # so the labels aren't grouped in blocks
gold = [{"id": i + 1, "text": x["text"], "label": x["label"]} for i, x in enumerate(gold)]

from collections import Counter
print("items:", len(gold), "| per label:", dict(Counter(x["label"] for x in gold)))

text:
Step 6 — Save it


Show code

Show code
import json
with open(OUT_FILE, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:   # open for writing
    json.dump(gold, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)   # list of dicts -> JSON text
print(f"Saved {len(gold)} items to {OUT_FILE}")
gold[:3]  # preview the first three items

text:
Step 3 — Reshape into the canonical schema
Two decisions:

Combine both files (both disciplines) into one dataset.
Expand the move codes into readable names (BAC→Background) and fit {id, text, label}.



Show code
### Step 3.1: translate the short move codes into readable names ###
CODES = {"BAC": "Background", "GAP": "Gap", "MTD": "Method",
         "PUR": "Purpose", "RST": "Result", "CLN": "Conclusion",
         "CTN": "Contribution", "IMP": "Implication"}

Step 2 — Look at the raw format
The Wiki-Auto files are tab-separated text, one sentence per line:
sentence <TAB> label_by_annotator_A <TAB> label_by_annotator_B
Labels are numbers: 1=A1, 2=A2, … 6=C2. Let’s print the first few raw lines.

title: CEFR-SP — download & preprocess
section: Step 3 — Reshape into the canonical schema
text:
Step 3 — Reshape into the canonical schema
Three decisions, each a real gold-standard-building choice:

Trust only agreement. We keep a sentence only when both annotators gave the same level — so every label is unambiguous (ideal for a first task).
Make labels human-readable. Convert 1→A1, …, 6→C2.
Fit the schema. Output {id, text, label}.



Show code
import glob

### Step 3.1: translate the numeric codes into readable CEFR levels ###
CEFR = {"1": "A1", "2": "A2", "3": "B1", "4": "B2", "5": "C1", "6": "C2"}

### Step 3.2: read every file line by line, keeping only what we can trust ###
rows = []
for path in glob.glob("CEFR-SP/CEFR-SP/Wiki-Auto/*.txt"):   # every .txt in there
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            parts = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")   # one line -> its 3 columns
            if len(parts) < 3:
                continue                       # a short line — skip it
            text, a, b = parts[0].strip(), parts[1].strip(), parts[2].strip()
            if text and a == b and a in CEFR:      # keep only agreed labels
                rows.append({"text": text, "label": CEFR[a]})

print("kept", len(rows), "agreed sentences")   # the rest were disagreements

title: CEFR-SP — download & preprocess
section: Step 7 — Also save the full pool
text:
Step 7 — Also save the full pool
Step 5 threw most of the data away on purpose: 12 items per level is the right size for a tutorial you hand-check. But the Day 3 prompt-tuning work and the final mini-project both want the whole thing — a larger set to draw fresh samples from, and items to use as few-shot examples that are not in your gold set.
So save every agreed sentence too, in the same schema. Same rows as Step 3, just numbered from 1.


Show code
POOL_FILE = "cefr_pool.json"

### Step 7.1: give every reshaped row an id, in order ###
pool = [{"id": i + 1, "text": x["text"], "label": x["label"]}
        for i, x in enumerate(rows)]

### Step 7.2: write it out ###
with open(POOL_FILE, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(pool, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)

from collections import Counter
print(f"Saved {len(pool)} items to {POOL_FILE}")
print("per label:", dict(Counter(x["label"] for x in pool)))


Note how unbalanced the pool is compared with your gold set — B1 and B2 dominate, A1 and C2 are scarce. That is what the real data looks like, and it is why Step 5 sampled evenly instead of just taking the first 72 rows.

Done! You built two files from raw research data:

cefr_sentences.json — the balanced 72-item gold set
cefr_pool.json — every agreed sentence (~3,200), to sample from later

⚠️ Both live in the Colab session and disappear when the runtime disconnects — save them to your Google Drive before you close the tab.
Next: use them in the Day 2 tutorial (annotation → evaluation) and the Day 3 tutorial (prompt design).

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis

📋 Agenda

Error analysis of misclassifications

A walkthrough of what run_prompt does internally

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
text:
🎯 Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Use show_errors to find misclassifications, hypothesize a fix, and re-run.
Compare macro-F1 across iteration rounds.
Place your result next to the published supervised results for the same corpus — and say what that comparison does and does not license.
State what supervised training gives you, and what it requires, compared with zero-training prompting.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
section: The number shows the change; the errors show the reason
text:
The number shows the change; the errors show the reason
macro-F1 went from 0.31 to 0.34. What changed?

You cannot answer that from the average. You have to look at what the model actually got wrong.


errors = show_errors(val, pred_cot)
errors.head(15)
Four columns: id · gold · pred · text.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
section: Read down the F1 column first
text:
Read down the F1 column first
evaluate already printed per-class F1. One or two levels will sit far below the rest.

That is where macro-F1 is being lost. Because macro-F1 weights every class equally, a rare class with F1 near zero lowers the average as much as a common one does.


Then read three actual sentences from that level. The counts show you where the problem is; the sentences show you what it is.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
text:
Two different causes






“The model is wrong”


The sentence is clearly B1, the model said C1, and your scheme is unambiguous about it. → a prompt problem










“The scheme is fuzzy”


You and your partner would also disagree about this sentence. → not fixable by prompting





Distinguishing these two cases is the most important analytic skill in your final report.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
section: The same change you already saw
text:
The same change you already saw
Back in S7, Huang & Mizumoto’s Ex 1 → Ex 2 was a generic prompt tightened into a structured one.

That is the same procedure as here, except that now the change is based on your error data, not on intuition:

read the errors (show_errors) — where does the prompt fail?
tighten one thing — usually the Criteria / label descriptors.
re-measure macro-F1 — did it actually help?







Tip


Change one thing per round, so you know what moved the number.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
section: Say what you expect, before you run it
text:
Say what you expect, before you run it
Three lines, filled in before you touch the prompt:
WORST_CLASS = "…"   # the level with the lowest F1
MY_CHANGE   = "…"   # the ONE thing you will change
I_PREDICT   = "…"   # what you expect, and why

This is what makes the work a study. A change that helps for a reason you stated in advance is a finding; a change that helps for no reason you can state is not.


An incorrect prediction does not lower your mark. Not stating a prediction at all does.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
section: Check the class you aimed at
text:
Check the class you aimed at
Macro-F1 can rise while the level you targeted gets worse, because a different class improved and raised the average.

So compare the F1 row for WORST_CLASS before and after, not only the macro-F1.













#
Change
Why I expected it to help
macro-F1
Target F1
Right?




0
(no change)
—
…
…
—


1
…
…
…
…
…



Two recorded rounds with stated reasons are worth more than five undocumented ones.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
text:
What run_prompt has been doing
We read the helper you have called all day. You do not edit it; the purpose is that you can describe what it does.


Insert each sentence at the {text} position → one prompt per item.
Call the model, paced so you stay under 15 requests/minute.
On a 429, wait and retry; on a daily quota error, stop immediately.
Scan the reply for the first CEFR level and keep it.
Return a plain list of labels, in gold order.



Step 4 is the step that most easily fails, which is why the CoT prompt forbids mentioning other levels.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
text:
How good is 0.36, really?
Arase, Uchida & Kajiwara (2022) — the paper behind this corpus — trained models on this exact task (their Table 6):



System
macro-F1
weighted κ




Bag-of-words + SVM
41.2
0.354


k-NN over frozen BERT
38.8
0.373


BERT-Base, loss-weighted
82.5
0.609


Their proposed model
84.5
0.628


Our zero-shot prompt (72 items)
≈36
0.849

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
section: Two readings you should not avoid
text:
Two readings you should not avoid
1. Zero-shot prompting scores near bag-of-words, not near BERT.
The difference up to 84.5 is what a labelled training set gives you. Building CEFR-SP required trained experts, and that is what such a training set costs.

2. Our weighted κ looks better than theirs. It is not.


Their test set is 3,012 sentences with the natural imbalance; ours is a balanced 72. κ is sensitive to the marginals.


A higher number obtained on a different test set is not a valid comparison, and your report must not make it.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
text:
What this licenses






Important


“The model got 0.36” means nothing until you can say 0.36 compared to what, on which items.




Claimable: “a zero-shot prompt reaches roughly bag-of-words performance on this task”.


Not claimable: “our prompt scored higher than the published model on agreement”.

title: Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis
text:
Assistant, not replacement
Neither approach is “the answer” — each has costs: data to train vs. a prompt to write, reproducibility, interpretability.

And back to where the running example started — Huang & Mizumoto (2025):

“Human teachers must ultimately remain at the core of language teaching and learning.”

The LLM is a tool you evaluate and supervise. You do not accept its output without checking it.

🎯 Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Split a paragraph into sentences two ways — naive .split(".") and a spaCy sentencizer — and explain why the naive rule fails.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
Same rhythm as Session 2

Slide for the idea, then do it in Colab.
Type it, don’t copy it.
In Part A you called the model once. Today you run it over many sentences, and write the Python that Days 2–5 are built from.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
The problem
Your data arrives as paragraphs. But the unit we work with is the sentence. So we need to segment a paragraph into its sentences.
The obvious idea: cut on every full stop. To do that we call a method on the string — some_text.split(".") — using a dot (.) to run a built-in action on that value.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
Why this matters
The naive rule works on simple text but fails on common cases: abbreviations and decimals contain dots that are not sentence ends.
Incorrect boundaries produce incorrect data in every later step, so it is worth seeing the naive rule fail before we use a better tool.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Let’s try — naive split
paragraph = ("Dr. Smith reviewed the data. The results were clear, "
             "e.g. accuracy rose. Scores went from 3.14 to 9.")

naive = paragraph.split(".")     # cut the string at every "."
print("pieces:", len(naive))     # how many pieces did that give us?
for piece in naive:              # look at each piece in turn
    print(repr(piece))           # repr() shows the quotes and spaces exactly

Look at the output: "Dr" (from Dr.), "e" and "g" (from e.g.), "3" and "14" (from 3.14) are all split in the wrong places. Sentence boundaries are not just full stops.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
Use an existing library
Instead of our own rule, we import a library built for this task, spaCy:
### Step 1: build a sentence splitter that knows more than "cut at every dot" ###
import spacy                       # the NLP toolbox
nlp = spacy.blank("en")            # a minimal English pipeline
nlp.add_pipe("sentencizer")        # add the rule-based splitter — no download

import spacy loads the library.
The sentencizer treats abbreviations and decimals correctly, not as sentence ends.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
Why this matters






Important


On Day 2, the sentence is the unit you annotate by hand and the unit you feed the LLM. Bad boundaries → bad gold data → misleading scores.



Correct segmentation is required for a correct gold standard: every label is attached to one segment.

This is your unit of analysis — the thing you attach one label to. Sometimes it’s the sentence (segment first, like here); sometimes it’s the whole text (an essay gets one rating). Session 4 formalizes this as sentence categorization vs text categorization.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Let’s try — the sentencizer
### Step 2: run it on the paragraph and look at what came out ###
doc = nlp(paragraph)               # spaCy reads the text
sentences = list(doc.sents)        # spaCy's sentence objects, as a list
for s in sentences:
    print(repr(s.text))

Compare to the naive split: Dr. Smith, e.g., and 3.14 stay intact. You now have a real list of sentences — exactly what the next section loops over.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
Why this matters
On Day 2 you build precision, recall, F1 and Cohen’s κ yourself, out of these seven pieces and nothing else.

Today is the only day of the course that teaches Python. Every pattern here is on the slide before you are asked to write it.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Step 3 — the loop
for sentence in examples:              # repeat everything below for each sentence
    prompt = f"What CEFR level (A1-C2) is this sentence? Answer with just the level. {sentence}"
    reply = ai.generate_text(prompt).strip()   # .strip() removes stray blank space
    if reply == "":                    # the model sometimes says nothing at all
        print(sentence, "→ (no answer)")
    else:                              # normal case: it answered
        print(sentence, "→", reply)

The f-string sits inside the loop, so the braces are filled in again for every sentence.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Step 4 — loop over records
Every dataset this week is a list of dicts. Each item is a record, so you reach in by key:
items = [{"id": 1, "text": "The cat sat on the mat.", "label": "A1"},
         {"id": 2, "text": "More research is needed.", "label": "B1"},
         {"id": 3, "text": "Nevertheless, the findings were inconclusive.",
          "label": "C1"}]

for item in items:                 # item is one record — a dict
    print(item["id"], "|", item["label"], "|", item["text"])

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Step 5 — build a list with .append
Often you don’t want to print each item — you want to keep something from it:
labels = []                        # start empty; the loop fills it
for item in items:
    labels.append(item["label"])   # add this item's label to the end

print(labels)                      # ['A1', 'B1', 'C1']

The most-used pattern of the week: Day 2 builds a list of verdicts this way, and the final project builds the list of rows your coders disagreed about.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Step 6 — count with a dict
The key is the label, the value is how many you have seen:
counts = {}                        # an empty dict: label -> how many
for item in items:
    label = item["label"]
    counts[label] = counts.get(label, 0) + 1   # count so far (0 if new), plus one

print(counts)                      # {'A1': 1, 'B1': 1, 'C1': 1}


counts[label] = ... — the same brackets you used to read a dict, now on the left of the =.
.get(label, 0) — reads the count so far, answering 0 when the label is new.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Step 7 — elif and and
elif adds branches: checked top to bottom, first match wins, exactly one runs.
for item in items:
    label = item["label"]
    if label == "A1" or label == "A2":     # `or` = either side is enough
        band = "basic"
    elif label == "B1" or label == "B2":   # only checked if the first did not match
        band = "independent"
    else:                                  # anything left over
        band = "proficient"
    print(label, "→", band)

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Step 7 — and, on two coders
A row counts as a disagreement only when both coders labelled it and the labels differ:
for row in rows:
    a = row["CoderA"]
    b = row["CoderB"]
    if a != "" and b != "" and a != b:   # both labelled it, AND they differ
        print(row["id"], "disagreement:", a, "vs", b)
    else:
        print(row["id"], "no disagreement")

A blank cell is not a disagreement — one coder simply hasn’t got there yet. That is a decision about your data, and on Day 2 you make it yourself.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Step 8 — divide, and guard
Counting leads to dividing: how many right, out of how many there were?
right = 9
wrong = 3
print(round(right / (right + wrong), 3))   # 0.75

If both counts are 0 there is nothing to divide by, and Python stops with ZeroDivisionError:
if right + wrong == 0:      # nothing was scored at all
    score = 0.0             # no credit — and no division by zero
else:
    score = right / (right + wrong)
Every score you write on Day 2 has this shape.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
section: 🧪 Step 9 — wrap it in a function
text:
🧪 Step 9 — wrap it in a function
You have written the same three steps twice. Name it once:
def ask(sentence):                     # `def` names a block of steps
    """Ask the model for the CEFR level of one sentence; return its reply."""
    prompt = f"What CEFR level (A1-C2) is this sentence? Answer with just the level. {sentence}"
    return ai.generate_text(prompt).strip()   # `return` hands the answer back

print(ask("The cat sat on the mat."))  # one line now does all three steps

print puts a value on the screen and it is gone; return hands it back, so you can store it, count it, or score it.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
Steps 5 and 9 together
Because ask hands its answer back, it goes straight into the loop from step 5:
replies = []
for sentence in examples:          # the three sentences from step 3
    replies.append(ask(sentence))  # call the function, keep what it returns

print(replies)

A list of sentences in, a list of the model’s labels out. That is the shape of Days 3 and 4 — and the result goes back into the record from Session 2, {"id", "text", "label"}, only now label comes from ask(...) instead of being typed by hand.

Mini-project setup

Form a group — each needs at least one Linguistic Data Analysis I alumnus.

Choosing now means your group is ready to start the project on Day 4. See the Final Project page for the tracks.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
If there is time
Nothing later in the week depends on this section. It is here because it makes the Session 1 slides runnable — you can look at the numbers a model keeps for each word, and see where they stop working.
The notebook has it at the very end, with its own download cell.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
One word, three hundred numbers
In Session 1 you saw that a model turns each word into a long list of numbers. You can look at that list.
word = nlp_vec("suggest")[0]      # read one word; [0] takes the first token
print("how many numbers:", word.vector.shape)
print("the first eight: ", word.vector[:8])

how many numbers: (300,)
the first eight:  [-0.126 -0.11  -0.61   0.105 -0.272  0.302 -0.014 -0.121]
Three numbers placed a colour in the Session 1 colour cube. It takes three hundred to place a word.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
Why this matters
Session 1 claimed that words with similar meanings end up with similar numbers. That claim is checkable, and you are about to check it.

It matters because the same claim has a limit, and the limit is the reason attention exists. Every category you annotate this week — a CEFR level, a rhetorical move, a hedged claim — depends on context. Finding where these vectors stop is what makes the rest of the week necessary.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
section: 🧪 Let’s try — how close are two words?
text:
🧪 Let’s try — how close are two words?
.similarity(...) compares two vectors: the higher the number, the closer the words sit.
print("suggest / indicate:", nlp_vec("suggest").similarity(nlp_vec("indicate")))
print("suggest / banana:  ", nlp_vec("suggest").similarity(nlp_vec("banana")))

suggest / indicate: 0.672
suggest / banana:   0.168
✏️ Your turn — swap in two words from your own research area.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
🧪 Let’s try — a word’s neighbours
Rather than guessing pairs, ask which words sit closest:
for neighbour in nearest("perhaps"):   # ✏️ your word here
    print(neighbour)

('possibly', 0.859)    ('might', 0.82)
('probably', 0.839)    ('rather', 0.817)
('certainly', 0.827)   ('though', 0.816)
('although', 0.825)    ('even', 0.812)
('however', 0.822)     ('maybe', 0.8)
Nothing told the model these words hedge a claim. They sit together because they turn up in the same positions in text.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
Now try nearest("corpus")
('habeas', 0.59)     ('textual', 0.534)
('christi', 0.572)   ('writ', 0.485)
('corpora', 0.566)   ('habeus', 0.465)

The legal sense, the religious sense and the linguistic sense are collected into one vector, because there is only one vector available for the spelling.
nearest("hedge") does the same with garden hedges and financial hedging.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
section: 🧪 Let’s try — where these vectors stop
text:
🧪 Let’s try — where these vectors stop
Session 1 used free in two sentences that mean different things:
banking = nlp_vec("your account is free of charge")
promo   = nlp_vec("claim your free prize now")

print("similarity:", banking[3].similarity(promo[2]))

similarity: 1.0
Not merely close — the same vector. One vector per word form, looked up the same way every time. That is what static means.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
…and word order is gone too
A sentence’s vector is the average of its words, and an average does not record their order:
print(nlp_vec("the dog chased the cat").similarity(nlp_vec("the cat chased the dog")))

1.0
Two sentences with opposite meanings, one score.






Important


This is the gap Session 1 said attention closes. A model built on these vectors alone cannot represent context; the model behind ai.generate_text(...) can.

title: Session 3: Python Practice & Mini-Project Setup
text:
A map of the space
map_words([...]) flattens 300 numbers onto a page, keeping close vectors close.
map_words(["perhaps", "possibly", "maybe", "likely", "presumably",
           "suggest", "indicate", "demonstrate", "argue", "conclude",
           "cat", "dog", "horse", "rabbit", "sheep"])   # ✏️ your words

The animals land well away from the rest. The hedges and the research verbs do not split into two groups — they are all academic prose words, appearing in similar places in similar texts, and that is the only thing these vectors record.


The map shows what the model separates, which is not always what you want it to separate.

title: Session 14: Project Work — Finalize Report & Notebook

🎯 Learning Objectives

title: Session 14: Project Work — Finalize Report & Notebook
section: Two different findings in one table
text:
Two different findings in one table
errors = show_errors(test, pred_final)     # the held-out half, from the frozen file
Four different findings live in that one table, and sorting them is the analysis:







model
the label is clear, both coders agreed at once, and the model still missed it


scheme
the item is genuinely borderline under your scheme


wording
the label name misleads — this one your next prompt could fix


ambiguous
the item is unclear in a way no scheme would settle










scheme and wording are the pair to be careful about


One is fixable by prompting and the other is not. Confusing them is how a group spends three rounds on a problem no prompt can reach.

title: Session 14: Project Work — Finalize Report & Notebook
text:
Overlap is a finding
overlap = errors_on_disagreed(errors, disagreed)   # disagreed: saved by 03
You already know which items are borderline, because you argued about them in Session 12. If the model’s errors cluster there, that is a result:

“The model’s B1/B2 confusions fall almost entirely on the 12 items our annotators also disagreed on. We read this as a property of the scheme’s boundary rather than a failure of the model.”


A sentence like this is worth more in your report than the F1 value itself.

title: Session 14: Project Work — Finalize Report & Notebook
text:
Be concrete






Weak


“The model struggled with C1.”









Strong


“id 6 — ‘Pseudogenes are generally thought of as the last stage…’ — gold C1, predicted C2. The sentence is syntactically simple but lexically dense; our scheme weights syntax, and the model appears to weight vocabulary. A scheme problem: our own coders disagreed on this item.”

title: Session 14: Project Work — Finalize Report & Notebook
section: The scaffold computes the numbers for you
text:
The scaffold computes the numbers for you
export_results fills in your label set, per-label counts, and the F1-per-round table.
Everything in italics is yours:

what your adjudication changed
the reason for each prompt change
the error attributions
limitations that apply to your run







Warning


A section left with the scaffold’s own text scores zero. make_submission.py warns you about this.

title: Session 14: Project Work — Finalize Report & Notebook
text:
Limitations that are actually yours






Generic (already in the scaffold)


“LLM output is stochastic.” · “Contamination risk.” · “Small sample.”









Yours


“Our C2 class has only 7 items because the pool contains 33 in total, so per-class C2 scores are effectively anecdotal.” · “We adjudicated 12 of 42 items, so our gold reflects two coders’ reading of an ambiguous boundary, not a settled one.”

title: Session 14: Project Work — Finalize Report & Notebook
text:
One command
python scripts/make_submission.py --group groupA
Keeps the folder structure — scripts/ · prompts/ · data/ · outputs/ — because that layout follows the S10 checklist, and because the notebook’s ../ paths require it.
Leaves out: .git/, .venv/, your .env, the large pool files, and anything from ICNALE.
Reports anything that is missing.

title: Session 14: Project Work — Finalize Report & Notebook
text:
Then check it reproduces






Restart the runtime and Run all


If your notebook only runs in the session where you built it cell by cell, it does not reproduce, and reproducibility is what you are claiming.




The bundle is self-contained for the claim you are making: given your gold set and your frozen predictions, anyone can recompute your numbers with no API key and no network access.

title: Session 14: Project Work — Finalize Report & Notebook
text:
Five slides
One per report section:

Scheme & gold
Prompt iterations
Evaluation
Error analysis
Limitations

Every group member speaks. Have your show_errors table open before you start.

title: Session 15: Final Presentations & Wrap-up
text:
📋 Agenda

8 min + 4 min Q&A per group
Course wrap-up

title: Session 15: Final Presentations & Wrap-up
text:
Format

Five slides, one per report section
Every member speaks to at least one slide
Confusion matrix on screen
show_errors table open and ready







Note


Your time is for the presentation, not for setting up. Have the notebook open before you start.

title: Session 15: Final Presentations & Wrap-up
section: The two questions every group gets
text:
The two questions every group gets






1


“Show us an item the model got wrong, and say whether the cause was the model or your scheme.”









2


“What did your QC pass change?”



Both questions ask about the analysis, not the code. They distinguish having run the cells from having done the work.

title: Session 15: Final Presentations & Wrap-up
text:
And a reminder






Your F1 is not graded


A study reporting 0.31 with a clear account of why scores higher than one reporting 0.82 without an account.
A low κ is not a penalty either. It is a finding about your scheme.

title: Session 15: Final Presentations & Wrap-up
section: What was the same in every track
text:
What was the same in every track
Whatever you annotated, the pipeline did not change:
load gold → format prompt → call model → evaluate → inspect errors

Only the task and the prompt changed. The pipeline is what transfers to your future work, not any particular model, which will be replaced within a year.

title: Session 15: Final Presentations & Wrap-up
text:
The one idea

An LLM produces annotations, and you must check them against a gold standard before you report them.


Checking means: a gold standard you built and can defend · a metric you understand because you once computed it by hand · a frozen run someone else can reproduce · and an accurate account of what your numbers do not show.


None of this is specific to LLMs. It is what makes any measurement worth reporting.

title: Session 15: Final Presentations & Wrap-up
text:
Where this goes next

Bigger gold sets — and inter-annotator agreement as a research question in its own right
Other constructs — anything you can define, you can try to annotate
The open questions — contamination, prompt sensitivity, whether “agreement with humans” is the right target at all


You now have a working pipeline and the practices needed to use it honestly. That is enough to begin your own work.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
📋 Agenda
We open with ten minutes in the Arase paper — pulling out the two design decisions S4 left for you. Then you build a gold standard for your track: the graded construction skill, split across three surfaces, with one shared sequence of steps (A–F) used on all of them:

These slides teach the concepts — how to sample, why annotate blind, how to read a matrix.
A Google Sheet holds the human judgment — you and your partner annotate there.
Colab does the numbers — import the Sheet, measure agreement, adjudicate, export.







Note


This is the construction skill — graded once, here. Give the annotation real care.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
🎯 Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Working in a pair, each annotate the same ~20 sentences by hand against a prepared scheme.
Read a function’s first line and its help(...) to work out what to pass in and what comes back.
Import the sheet into Colab and compute percent agreement, Cohen’s κ, and an annotator-vs-annotator confusion matrix.
Read the confusion matrix to see where you disagree, then refine the scheme and re-annotate — iterate until agreement is acceptable.
Adjudicate the remaining disagreements, compare to the published gold, and interpret the differences.
Export your annotations as a canonical {id, text, label} gold set.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
Two decisions, ten minutes
S4 ended on the two decisions the summary table skipped — and they are the two you make today:

Which sentences go into the pool? → your step A
Who is allowed to annotate them? → your step C


In pairs, with the two excerpts (§3.2 and §3.1): fill the worksheet. You are scanning for specifics — a number, a criterion, a reason — not reading for comprehension. 7 minutes.






Note


Everything on the sheet is stated explicitly in the excerpt except the last row, which asks you to reason. Don’t read past the first paragraph of each.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
The worksheet








#
Question





1
How many candidate annotators were recruited? How many were kept?
→ C


2
What exactly did each candidate do, to be screened?
→ C


3
Two criteria decided who was kept. Both — not just the obvious one.
→ C


4
Why use only the first sentence of a paragraph?
→ A


5
Name two things that got a sentence thrown out.
→ A


6
They already had 17k sentences from two corpora. Why add a third (SCoRE)?
→ A









Tip


Q3 and Q6 are the ones worth arguing about with your partner. Write something for both.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
Who is allowed to annotate
Their claim: sentence CEFR level can be judged objectively — but only by someone with teaching experience. So they tested that before trusting anyone.

Pilot — 228 sentences. Against a senior expert (12 yrs teaching): a CEFR-trained grad student reached r = 0.74. Three grad students with no CEFR and no teaching background: 0.45 / 0.50 / 0.59.
Trial — 8 candidates, the same 100 sentences, scored against the expert’s labels. Agreement ran 0.59–0.77 — and roughly tracked years and type of teaching experience.
Kept 2, on two criteria: high agreement (r = .75, .73) and small average level difference (0.11, 0.22).







Note


Why both? Correlation asks do you rank sentences the same way. Mean difference asks are you calibrated — a rater who is consistently one grade high correlates almost perfectly.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
Which sentences are allowed in
The rule: if you need anything outside the sentence to judge it, the sentence doesn’t belong.
“The white house announced his return.” — easy words, easy grammar. But you must know the White House is an organisation, and resolve his from the sentence before. That’s world knowledge and discourse, not sentence difficulty.

First sentence of a paragraph only → nothing to co-refer back to.
No named entities, quotations or brackets — though dates, numbers and famous places are allowed.
5–30 words, then sampled at random.
A third source on purpose: Newsela-Auto + Wiki-Auto (8.5k each) — plus SCoRE (3.0k), written for beginners, because A-level sentences are otherwise almost absent.







Tip


These filters were not decided in advance — the authors ran several rounds of manual checks over a few hundred samples before fixing them. Sampling rules are revised as you test them.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
section: And what came out of it
text:
And what came out of it
Sentences the annotators agreed on in the pilot and trial became the example per level in the guidelines — so selecting people also produced the scheme’s anchors (Arase et al., Table 1):







CEFR Level
Example sentence




A1
She had a beautiful necklace around her neck.


A2
Some experts say the classes should be changed.


B1
Historically there have also been negative consequences.


B2
Alligators are generally timid towards humans and tend to walk or swim away if one approaches.


C1
The metal-carbon bond in organometallic compounds is generally highly covalent.


C2
In the past, non-photosynthetic plants were mistakenly thought to get food by breaking down organic matter in a manner similar to saprotrophic fungi.









Tip


Not just word difficulty — grammar, abstraction and world knowledge also increase across the levels. This is the judgment you’re about to make. Their own two experts matched exactly 37.6% of the time — so expect to differ, from your partner and from the gold.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
Today’s goal, as six steps (A–F)
Your goal: build a gold standard for your track, and know how far you can trust it. That is phase ③ (Eguchi & Kyle Step 6) — broken into six steps. The same A–F labels appear on every surface, so you always know where you are: find your place by the letter, not the slide number.








Step
Where you work
What happens




A · Sample
slide + Sheet
concept: how to draw a representative ~20; you copy your track’s sheet


B · Apply the scheme
slide + guidelines
restate the decidable rule you’ll annotate against


C · Annotate blind
Sheet
each partner labels the same items, independently


D · Measure agreement
Colab + slide
% agreement · Cohen’s κ · annotator-vs-annotator matrix


E · Read → refine → re-annotate
slide + Sheet
where do you diverge? fix the scheme, re-label


F · Adjudicate → gold
Colab + slide
resolve, compare to published, export {id,text,label}










Tip


You move to the Sheet twice (annotate in C, re-annotate in E) and then return. Colab opens at D and stays open. The slides run alongside as your interpretation reference.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
section: Draw a sample that stands for the domain
text:
Draw a sample that stands for the domain
A gold standard is only as trustworthy as the sample it’s built on. Before anyone labels anything, decide what you’re drawing.

Representative — cover the range you care about (proficiency, L1, register), so your κ does not come from an unusually easy subset.
Right-sized — enough to measure agreement, small enough to double-annotate by hand (~20 today).
Reproducible — a fixed random seed gives the same 20 items every time; anyone can draw your exact sample again.
One fixed unit — one label per unit of analysis (here, the sentence). Decide this before you start.
Exclusions — Arase’s first-sentence-only, no named entities rule, which you just found. Anything that must be judged from outside the sentence does not belong in the pool.







Note


Today the sample is already drawn for you — one sheet per track. You’ll learn how it was sampled here, and just copy it in a moment. (The draw itself lives in Colab as a reference cell.)

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
section: Restate the rule before you label
text:
Restate the rule before you label
You already have an operationalized scheme from the earlier sessions — a decidable rule a second person can follow. Now you apply it.

Restate the rule and the unit — one label per unit; know your label set cold.
Skim the guidelines and per-level examples before you annotate, not while you annotate.
Do not invent rules while annotating — if the scheme cannot decide a case, write it down for step E instead of deciding it privately.

This is ① and ② made concrete: a decidable rule, applied to a real sample.






Copy your track’s sheet, then go annotate


Open your track’s template Sheet → File → Make a copy into your own Drive. Note the copied title — Colab needs it in step D. Then move to step C.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
section: Two people, the same items, independently
text:
Two people, the same items, independently
This is the central step of the session, and it happens entirely in the Sheet — no code.

Each partner labels the same ~20 items in the sheet you copied.
Two annotator columns (label_a, label_b) → agreement falls straight out in step D.
Blind = do not look at your partner’s column, and do not discuss items while you label.

The disagreements are what you need: they show where the scheme is still unclear. Do not resolve them yet.






Note


Your turn: label all ~20 rows in your own column, independently. Use the notes column for anything you found genuinely hard to decide — those notes are your evidence in step E.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
section: First: reading a helper’s first line
text:
First: reading a helper’s first line
Colab opens here, and you start calling helpers someone else wrote. Their first line tells you what to pass in.
def to_canonical(rows: list[dict[str, str]],
                 labels: list[str],
                 column: str = COL_FINAL) -> list[dict[str, str]]:


rows, labels, column — what the arguments are called.
After each colon, the kind of data it expects: rows is a list of dicts, labels is a list of text, column is one piece of text.
= COL_FINAL — column already has a value, so you can leave it out.
After the ->, what you get back. -> None means it only prints something.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
Asking Colab
You do not have to open the helper cell to see this.
help(to_canonical)

Colab prints the first line, then a written description of every argument and of what comes back. Typing to_canonical( and pressing Shift+Tab shows the same thing in a pop-up.








Tip


You never write these yourself. You read them so you know what to pass in.



→ try this in step D (Colab), just above the first load_annotation_sheet call.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
Percent agreement vs. Cohen’s κ
Now Colab opens for the first time. It reads your sheet and reports three numbers — but the reading of them happens here.


Percent agreement — the raw diagonal. Simple, but it gives a high score too easily: two coders who both say “B1” most of the time will agree often by chance.
Cohen’s κ — agreement corrected for chance. Report this one.









Tip


Recall from S4: 80% raw agreement was only κ ≈ 0.52 once chance was removed.



→ run this in step D (Colab): load_annotation_sheet → calc_percentage_agreement → calc_cohen_kappa.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
Read the confusion matrix
The κ tells you how much you disagree. The annotator-vs-annotator confusion matrix tells you where.


Rows = annotator A, columns = annotator B — one cell per label pair.
The diagonal is where you agreed; off-diagonal cells are your disagreements.
Many items in one off-diagonal cell (say B1 ↔︎ B2) indicates that that boundary is under-defined in your scheme.



Do not stop at κ is low. Find the specific label pair that produces most of the disagreement. That cell is your task list for step E.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
section: Fix the scheme, then label again
text:
Fix the scheme, then label again
A confusion matrix does not evaluate you as an annotator. It shows which parts of your scheme are unclear.


Take the off-diagonal cells — which label pairs get confused?
Refine the scheme / guidelines so that ambiguity becomes decidable (add a rule, a boundary case, an example).
Re-annotate the affected items; recompute κ. Iterate until agreement is acceptable.



This is Fuoli’s principle 2 in action — guidelines are tested and refined until reliable. If two trained coders still can’t agree, no model can be trusted on it either.






Re-annotate in a fresh round tab


Make your scheme edits, then duplicate the round1 tab → round2 and re-label the confused items there — never overwrite round1. Back in Colab, disagreements(rows) lists what to revisit; set ROUND = "round2" and re-run step D to see κ move. Each round is preserved, so the analysis stays reproducible and you can see how κ changes from round to round.

title: Session 5: Hands-on: Gold-Standard Annotation & Agreement
text:
Resolve, compare, export
The remaining disagreements cannot be removed by refining the scheme. You decide them. That is adjudication, and it is the graded step.


Talk through the remaining disagreements and agree a single final label for each.
Compare to the published gold — where do you differ, and why? A difference isn’t automatically an error.
Export the canonical {id, text, label} set — this is what S6 measures the model against, and the input to ④⑤.









Note


Differing from the published gold ≠ being wrong. Arase’s own experts agreed exactly only 37.6% of the time. What matters is that your disagreement is defensible — that’s the argument your mini-project has to make.



→ run this in step F (Colab): to_canonical → compare_to_published → save to Drive.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
📋 Agenda
For three days you have checked an LLM’s output against a gold standard. Today: how to report the result honestly.

Reproducibility — pin · log · temperature=0 + seed · freeze
Limits — hallucination, data contamination, stochasticity
Ethics — privacy, authorship, and what a licence actually asks of you
The reporting checklist — the five sections you will hand in







Note


This is the switch from tutorial mode to project mode. Everything after this session is your own study.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
🎯 Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Name the four practices that make an LLM result reproducible, and apply them to your own run.
Explain why temperature=0 is not sufficient, and what freezing your predictions adds.
Say which of hallucination, contamination and stochasticity your own track is exposed to.
Apply the five-section reporting checklist — including saying what your numbers do not show.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
The problem, stated plainly
You run your prompt and get F1 = 0.62. Tomorrow you run the same prompt and get 0.58.

Which number goes in the report?


Neither, until you can say why they differ. A result you cannot reproduce is not yet a finding.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
Four practices









Practice
Why




1
Pin the model + version
gemini-3.1-flash-lite ≠ gemini-2.5-flash. Models are silently retired and replaced.


2
Log the prompt
as a file, versioned — not a string you overwrote


3
temperature=0 + a fixed seed
removes the sampling randomness you control


4
Save the predictions to a file
removes the variation you cannot control

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
Why temperature=0 is not enough
temperature=0 says “always take the most likely next token.” That should be deterministic.

It mostly is. But you are calling a hosted service:

the model behind the name can be updated underneath you
batching and hardware differences perturb floating-point arithmetic
the endpoint may silently fall back to another region



So a hosted LLM is only best-effort reproducible. You cannot fix this; it is a property of using a hosted service.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
section: The solution: run once, then save the output
text:
The solution: run once, then save the output
predictions = run_prompt(PROMPT, gold)          # ← the ONE run
save_predictions(predictions, "outputs/cefr_groupA_predictions.json")
From then on, every number comes out of that file:
pred_final = load_predictions("outputs/cefr_groupA_predictions.json")
evaluate(gold, pred_final, ordered=True)        # the same answer every time

You did this on Day 2 — you loaded a frozen predictions file we made for you, which is why the whole class got identical numbers. Now you make your own.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
What freezing gives you

A stable number — your reported F1 does not change while you write the report.
No quota use — re-running the analysis makes no further model calls.
Recomputable by others — anyone, including whoever grades it, can recompute your numbers from exactly the outputs you saw.







Important


The third point is the important one. “Reproducible” does not mean you can get the number again. It means someone else can.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
Three failure modes
Hallucination — the model produces fluent output that is incorrect.
Data contamination — the model may have seen your test data in training.
Stochasticity — the same input gives different outputs.

For a classification task like yours, the first is limited because the label set is closed, and you have just handled the third. The second is the one that affects your claims.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
Contamination: why it matters here
Every track you can pick uses a published dataset.

CEFR-SP is on GitHub. RAAMove is on GitHub. CaRS-50 is on Mendeley. AutoErrorAnalyzer is on OSF.
These were all published before the model’s training cutoff.


So when the model labels a sentence correctly, there are two explanations:

it understands the construct
it has seen this sentence with this label before



You cannot distinguish these two explanations from your F1 alone. State this in your report.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
What you can honestly claim






Not claimable


“Gemini can annotate CEFR level with F1 = 0.62.”









Claimable


“On 42 items from CEFR-SP, with this prompt and this model version, macro-F1 was 0.62. The corpus is public and predates the model’s training cutoff, so contamination cannot be ruled out.”



The second sentence is easier to defend and more useful to a reader.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
Three things worth ten minutes
Privacy. Learner data is people’s writing. ICNALE is licensed for research use only and may not be redistributed — which is why it is excluded from git and from your submission bundle by name.
Authorship. The model is a tool, not a co-author. But what it did belongs in your methods: which model, which prompt, which parameters.
Licences have practical consequences. CEFR-SP is CC BY-SA: anything you redistribute from it inherits share-alike. That is why the template’s data folder carries its own LICENSE file.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
section: A limitation of your own study
text:
A limitation of your own study
You are about to measure a model against a gold standard built by two of you, on 40 items, in 25 minutes.

That is a small gold standard, built quickly, and it contains errors.


So is most of the published literature. The difference between good and bad work here is not the size of the gold set — it is whether you say what it was.

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
Five sections









Section
The thing that makes it good




1
Scheme & gold
what adjudication changed


2
Prompt iterations
a reason per round, not just an F1


3
Evaluation
which class did worst, and what it got confused with


4
Error analysis
model error or unclear scheme — with evidence


5
Limitations
≥2 that apply to your run

title: Session 10: Methodology — Reproducibility, LLM Limits & Ethics
text:
How the report is graded






Your F1 is not graded


A careful study reporting F1 = 0.31 with a clear account of why scores higher than a sloppy one reporting 0.82.




The reason is that a number you cannot explain is not a finding, and that distinction is what the whole course is about.


So pick the track that will teach you something, not the one that will produce a high score. cars50 is the hardest track because its own annotators only reached κ ≈ 0.43, which makes it the best track for showing that you can distinguish “the model is wrong” from “the scheme is unclear”.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
text:
📋 Agenda
You work in Colab for this whole session, on your own track and your own data.

20 min — sample a balanced subset, create the annotation sheet
25 min — annotate blind, two of you, independently
30 min — agreement → the disagreement rule you write → adjudicate
5 min — draw the dev/test line







Important


PLAN.md signed first. Steps 1–2 need no model, so nothing is blocked while you wait.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
text:
🎯 Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Draw a balanced subset and explain why balance matters for P/R/F1 and the matrix.
Annotate independently and blind, and say which agreement statistics your design owes.
Write the rule that decides what counts as a disagreement, and defend the one you chose.
Adjudicate disagreements into one agreed gold set, and record what changed.
Split that gold set into dev and test, and defend the ratio.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
text:
Pool vs. sample
A pool is everything the corpus has, with its natural imbalance:
cefr_pool.json → A1: 51 · A2: 246 · B1: 1229 · B2: 1188 · C1: 436 · C2: 33

A sample is what you study — equal items per label:
sampled = sample_pool(pool, N_PER_CLASS, SEED)
# Sampled 42 items. Per-label counts: {'A1': 7, 'A2': 7, ... 'C2': 7}

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
text:
Why balance
With 1229 B1s and 33 C2s, a model that answers “B1” to every item gets a high accuracy score without using any information.
Balanced sampling makes per-class precision and recall readable, and makes the confusion matrix show which labels are confused with which instead of showing the class sizes.







Note


Rare classes give you fewer items. That is a property of the data, and it belongs in your limitations section.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
text:
Why keep the pool separate
The items you did not sample have a purpose: they become your few-shot examples in 04_develop.
If your examples came from your gold set, the model would be given the answers to the items you are about to test it on.

build_fewshot prevents this for you, but only if items remain in the pool. Sample from the full pool, not the demo file.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
section: The step you must do yourself
text:
The step you must do yourself
The published labels are somebody else’s judgment.

Before you measure a model against them, two of you re-annotate the sample independently and blind. You then measure how far apart you were, and discuss every item you labelled differently.


These are the same A–F steps you did by hand in Session 5, now on your own track.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
text:
What “blind” means here
create_annotation_sheet deliberately does not copy the published label across.
| ID | Text                          | CoderA | CoderB | Final | Note |
|----|-------------------------------|--------|--------|-------|------|
| 1  | Bears do not have good hearing|        |        |       |      |

CoderA and CoderB fill their own columns without looking at each other’s. Final stays empty until you have talked.






Tip


The Sheet is a real Google Sheet, so all group members can work in it at the same time.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
section: Then measure — and you write these lines
text:
Then measure — and you write these lines
rows = load_coder_sheets(SHEET_ID, CODERS)   # one tab per coder, joined by ID

a = column(rows, CODERS[0])
b = column(rows, CODERS[1])

percent_agreement(a, b)                      # 71.4%
print(cohen_kappa_score(a, b))               # 0.657

Which κ you owe is not a free choice, and it is settled before you run anything — by how many coders you have and by whether PLAN.md §3 says your labels are a scale. Two coders, unordered: cohen_kappa_score(a, b). On a scale: weights="quadratic" as well. Three or more: fleiss_kappa.
Both numbers, not one. Percent agreement alone counts lucky agreement as if you had earned it; κ alone is hard to read without the raw figure beside it. They go in report section 1.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
section: What counts as a disagreement? — you write that too
text:
What counts as a disagreement? — you write that too
disagreements is not given to you, because the rule inside it is a decision about your scheme:
disagreed = disagreements(rows, coders=CODERS)   # your function

A row is a disagreement when your coders did not all choose the same label — that is the obvious rule. On labels that sit on a scale, you may decide only a gap of two or more is worth arguing about. Both are defensible; which you used is a sentence in your report.






Tip


You saw these six lines on Day 2 S5, step E. answer("disagreements") is there if you stall.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
text:
Adjudicate
The 12 rows you disagreed on are not random error. They are the places where your scheme is unclear, and they are usually the same places where the model makes errors.

For each: agree a Final label, and note why. Then:
rows = load_coder_sheets(SHEET_ID, CODERS)          # re-read: Final is filled in now
gold = to_canonical(rows, LABELS, source=sampled)   # puts back what the sheet drops
compare_to_published(gold, sampled)
# 37 / 42 match the published label (88.1%)


Those 5 differences are a finding about the corpus, not an error on your part.

The consequence






Your adjudicated gold is what the model gets scored against


Not the published labels.



This is why this session matters. The label boundaries you discuss here are the ones you will refer to on Day 5, in 06_report, when you explain the model’s errors.

text:
Which items you may look at
Tomorrow you will change your prompt because of what you saw it get wrong. That is the work. But a score measured on the items you kept adjusting against stops measuring how good your prompt is, and starts measuring how long you kept adjusting.

So the line gets drawn now, before anything has been run against these items:








what it is for




dev
the items you may look at. Iterate here, as many rounds as you like


test
opened once, in 05_test.ipynb. Whatever it says is what you report

text:
The split
dev, test = split_dev_test(gold, DEV, seed=SEED)

save_json(dev,  DEV_PATH,  what="dev items")
save_json(test, TEST_PATH, what="test items")
Read the per-label counts it prints before you save. A label that lands in dev but not in test cannot appear in the score you report, and this is the last cheap moment to change dev: in config.yaml and draw the line again.






Note


This is the loop you wrote by hand this morning, in Day 4 Part B — bucket by label, take some of each. One call now.

title: Session 12: Project Work — Sample & QC the Gold Set
text:
dev is the fast set






You do not shrink your sample to iterate


One round on the dev half — a dozen or so items — is about a minute of enforced pacing. Your sample stays at full size all the way through, and the number you finally report comes off the test half, which nothing has touched.



There is no right ratio at this size, only one you can defend. A bigger dev gives steadier feedback and leaves a smaller test, so the reported number bounces more. A smaller dev means prompt decisions made on very few items — which is how you tune to noise.

🎯 Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Name the four prompt elements — instruction · context · input data · output indicator — and locate each in a real prompt.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
section: A prompt has parts you can design
text:
A prompt has parts you can design
An LLM does what the prompt tells it to. Change the prompt and you change the output, and the score.

A prompt is not a fixed phrase that you either know or do not know. It has parts you can design deliberately, and today we learn those parts on one concrete example.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
text:
Four elements of a prompt
Chen et al. (2023), via Huang & Mizumoto (2025) — an effective prompt typically has four parts:

Instruction — what the model should do (start with a verb: classify, summarize, explain).
Context — the background, role, rubric, or level that scopes the task.
Input data — the actual text to be processed.
Output indicator — the form of the answer (format, tone, “only feedback, no rewrite”).


If one of the four is missing, the output is usually not what you wanted.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
text:
Sharpening the instruction — structure & persona
The instruction element has the largest effect, so write it carefully:

Start with a verb and be specific — “classify this sentence into one CEFR level (A1–C2)” is more effective than “tell me about this sentence.”
Give it a persona / role — “You are an experienced EFL writing tutor…” sets the tone, standards, and vocabulary of the output.


A persona helps, but it changes style, not knowledge. The four elements have the larger effect.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
text:
The running example — writing feedback
Huang & Mizumoto’s Example Prompt 2 — a structured paragraph-feedback prompt for an EFL class:

Task — Based on the following criteria, review the following paragraph and provide specific feedback… I am not seeking rewrite, give me only feedback.
Criteria — 1. Hook / Attention-grabber · 2. Background / Context · 3. Thesis statement · 4. Organization · 5. Clarity & coherence
My paragraph — (paste your paragraph here)


Read the four elements straight off it:



Element
In this prompt




Instruction
“review… and provide specific feedback”


Context
the 5-item Criteria rubric


Input data
“My paragraph”


Output indicator
“only feedback, no rewrite”

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
text:
Zero-shot vs. few-shot

Zero-shot — instruction only, no examples. The model relies on what it already knows. Great for simple, familiar tasks.
Few-shot — you include a few worked examples (input → correct label) right in the prompt, so the model infers the pattern.


When do examples help? When the task is specialized, the label set is your own, or the format must be exact. Two tips (promptingguide.ai):

keep a consistent format across all examples;
make the examples’ label space representative — don’t show only one class.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
section: What examples actually buy — Kim & Lu (2024)
text:
What examples actually buy — Kim & Lu (2024)
A hard linguistic task: labelling rhetorical move-steps in research-article introductions (modified Swales CARS: 3 moves / ~17 steps) with GPT-3.5. Unit of annotation = the sentence.

They tested two independent variables:

zero-shot vs. three-shot — the prompt alone vs. the prompt + 3 fully annotated introductions (38 sentences, drawn from the training set — not the gold test set).
initial vs. refined prompt — the instruction sharpened after reading the validation-set confusion matrix.







Important


Notice: the few-shot examples come from training, never from the gold set you score on. (More on this shortly.)

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
section: The numbers — prompting alone stops improving
text:
The numbers — prompting alone stops improving
Test-set accuracy, move / step (their Table 2):


  initial promptrefined prompt
  zero-shot
    42.9% / 17.0%
    50.5% / 19.8%
  three-shot
    46.2% / 18.7%
    52.7% / 25.3%

Fine-tuning on 80 samples → 92.3% / 80.2% — far above the best prompt (the S12 escalation).

Each change helps a little, and refined + three-shot is best. But prompting alone reaches only about 53% move accuracy, well below fine-tuning.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
text:
Four things the numbers teach

Few-shot helps, but modestly — adding 3 examples to the initial prompt was not significant on its own (McNemar move χ²=0.543, p=0.46).
Examples and instructions compound — only refined + three-shot beat the zero-shot baseline significantly (move p=0.028, step p=0.018). Sharpen the instruction and add examples.
Few-shot mainly raises recall — precision was higher than recall, and examples raised recall. (That precision/recall relationship returns in S8/S9.)
Context-heavy tasks need more than prompting — the best prompt-only setting was still far below fine-tuning: prompt first, and consider fine-tuning when prompting stops improving.







Note


Discuss: When would 3 well-chosen examples beat a longer instruction? How do you pick which examples to show? Why might few-shot raise recall but not precision?

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
text:
Chain-of-thought (CoT)
Ask the model to reason in steps before answering (Wei et al., 2022).
Huang & Mizumoto’s Example Prompt 1 is CoT feedback:

First, read the paragraph to understand its main idea. Next, check the structure… Then, identify grammatical errors. After that, assess clarity and coherence. Provide feedback based on these steps.


Zero-shot CoT is often just one added line — “Let’s think step by step” (Kojima et al., 2022).






Tip


CoT helps on tasks that need several judgements in sequence, such as reviewing writing or deciding a borderline label.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
text:
Iterating a prompt: Ex 1 → Ex 2
The same feedback task, tightened:

Ex 1 (generic) — “give feedback on this paragraph, step by step.” Works, but vague.
Ex 2 (structured) — split into Task / Criteria / My paragraph, add the output indicator “only feedback.”


That change — generic → structured — is prompt iteration. The data-based version is error analysis: find where the model is wrong (the confusion matrix), make the Criteria that cause those errors more precise, and the score rises. This is the same as Kim & Lu’s initial → refined change. You will do this yourself in S9.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
section: Run it this week vs. know it exists
text:
Run it this week vs. know it exists







Run it in S8
Know it exists (name & reason, don’t run)




zero-shot
self-consistency — sample N answers, take the majority (relevant to reproducibility → S10)


few-shot
RAG — give the model the annotation manual / codebook to consult (≈ dynamic few-shot)


chain-of-thought
agentic / multi-step — the model plans → critiques its own label → revises


structured output
(ReAct, Reflexion, prompt chaining…)




A reference for all of these: promptingguide.ai/techniques.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
section: Two errors to avoid before you tune
text:
Two errors to avoid before you tune

Train/test contamination — never draw your few-shot examples from the gold set you score on. The model would then be given the answers to the test items.
Validation vs. test — tune the prompt on a small validation set; report the final number once on a held-out test set.


Both protect the purpose of an evaluation: an accurate estimate of how the prompt performs on text it has not seen.

title: Session 7: Prompt Design: Zero-shot vs Few-shot
section: S8 — the same four elements, a new task
text:
S8 — the same four elements, a new task
Next session you build a real classification pipeline — and the CEFR prompt is the same four elements:







Ex 2 (feedback)
CEFR classification (S8)




Instruction: “provide feedback”
“classify this sentence’s CEFR level”


Context: the 5-item rubric
the CEFR level descriptors


Input: “My paragraph”
the learner sentence


Output indicator: “only feedback”
“return only the label” → JSON




S8 — run zero → few → CoT on CEFR, with a Gemini API key. S9 — read the errors, iterate, and benchmark against a trained model.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Course Description
Large Language Models (LLMs) — generative AI technologies that produce human-like language — have become one of the common tools people rely on. Linguistic research is no exception: more and more researchers are exploring the potential of this technology to support various stages of their work. One promising application of LLMs is linguistic annotation, a task that can be highly resource-intensive. If the annotation process can be supported by LLMs, the research community can benefit from greater scalability. Lowering the barriers to linguistic annotation is especially important for graduate research, where individual student researchers often have limited resources. Yet, while LLMs hold promise for linguistic research, the adequacy of model outputs must be critically evaluated rather than assumed. We must therefore be equipped with approaches to critically appraise what they can and cannot offer in order to make meaningful contributions to the field. In this course, we cover the foundational concepts and methods for evaluating LLM outputs in linguistic research projects.

Agenda

Why this course — LLMs are now common tools, and they are already changing how science is written. Annotation is the promising and expensive application, so the question is how to judge whether an LLM is doing it well.
Self-introductions — your name, your research interest, and why you took this course.
Syllabus — the course objectives, the 5-day map, and how you are assessed.
What an LLM is — what you already know about them, a 7-minute overview video, and the three questions we come back to: what the model predicts, where its numbers come from, and what attention does.
A brief history of embeddings — vectors and the RGB colour space, the distributional hypothesis, co-occurrence counts, Latent Semantic Analysis, word2vec, and finally the Transformer and self-attention. This is how text becomes numbers, and how one word gets a different representation in each context.
What LLM can be used, and where it fails — what an LLM lets you annotate that earlier methods could not, why sounding right is not being right, what people have already published using LLMs as annotators, and which part of NLP this course covers (evaluation, not training).
Discussion — what was new, and whether you come out of it optimistic or skeptical.

Bring a laptop today. This session is lecture and discussion, but Sessions 2 and 3 this afternoon are hands-on in Google Colab. If you have not set Colab up yet, work through the Google Colab setup guide before Session 2.
